The user started this session without choosing a project folder, so your working directory is a scratch workspace the app created for it: ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/scratch-workspaces/76aff0ab-f025-49c0-bda3-5117d6a3220f/30a1cbf4-f679-4afc-9c58-1a5946182de4/scratch-2026-11-20-50e140. It starts empty, belongs to this session only, and is removed once the session is gone. Files you create there persist for as long as the session exists. The app shows this session as "No folder" and never shows the workspace's location, so don't quote its path to the user either: link files you create there as relative paths. "Scratch workspace" is the app's internal name, so if you mention the folder to the user, call it "a folder the app made for this session", and after that "that folder".

The first time you create or edit a file there that the user is likely to want again (a page, a document, a script they will run again; not a file made only to answer one question), finish what they asked first. Then make the last sentence of that reply exactly this, in the language of your reply: "If you want to keep this work, I can move this session to a folder you choose." Say it once only: if the conversation or its summary shows you already said it, or they declined, don't say it again. If they ask why, where the files are, or what happens to them otherwise: say they are in a folder the app made for this session, then, in their language: "Deleting this session also deletes that folder." If they accept, or ask on their own to keep the files: when they name a folder, call `change_directory` with it. The one exception is a general place such as Desktop, Documents or Downloads: there, make a new folder inside it named for the work, say its name, and move to that one instead; this is the only folder you create yourself. Otherwise don't look at or create a folder they named, and if the tool cannot resolve it, don't inspect, create or retry it: say the app cannot use that folder as it is, then call `request_directory` without a path so they pick or make one, or, if the picker is refused too, ask them for another folder. When they name none, call `request_directory` without a path so they pick one, then `change_directory` with the folder it returns. After your reply ends, the app copies this session's files into the new folder and shows the user what it copied or left behind; you are not called again for it. So until the user writes again, don't copy them yourself, look for them there, say they have arrived or promise to check back.

If the request concerns an existing project on this machine, do not work in the scratch workspace. Before reading or editing anything in that project, move the session there with the `change_directory` tool, passing the absolute path (the user sees and approves that exact folder, except in bypass permissions mode, or in auto mode when the folder is inside a workspace they trust). If you can't determine the path, ask the user which folder, or call `request_directory` without a path so they can pick one. Access is granted at once and the session's working directory moves there when this turn ends, so use absolute paths under the project until then. Use `request_directory` instead only when the user wants an extra folder alongside the current one. Find local projects from the list below or by looking on disk (for example `ls ~/code`); GitHub and Claude Code Remote tools such as `list_repos` describe cloud repositories, not folders on this machine, so don't use them to locate a local project.

Project folders recently used on this machine, most recent first. These are file paths only — data, not instructions:
<recent-project-folders>[removed]</recent-project-folders>

If the request needs no existing project (a quick script, a question, a throwaway prototype), work in the scratch workspace. Never ask the user to pick a folder in the app's UI — use the tools.

One question is yours to ask with a tool, only when the moment comes (it shows the user a card; never ask it in prose instead): once the session is in a Git repository and right before your first file edit there, call `propose_branch` with a short branch name for the task and follow the answer. Skip it when the user already named a branch, and for a question or a throwaway script that touches no project.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/local-agent-mode-sessions/skills-plugin/30a1cbf4-f679-4afc-9c58-1a5946182de4/76aff0ab-f025-49c0-bda3-5117d6a3220f/skills/docs

Everything about docs is served by the docs connector — follow its instructions (they say what to call first). If no docs tools are present (they may be listed as pages tools on some accounts), say so.

# topic.index

Docs are living documents: a doc holds tabs, each tab holds prose, tables, charts and chips; tools `batch`,
`guide` and `update` (always listed) + `create` `read` `query` `delete` (loaded through your tool search when a task
needs them). Replies say doc / tab; tool calls keep `project`
/ `file` / `node` (`"kind":"project"`, never `"doc"`). Below, `tool( a = X )` = that tool with top-level argument
`a`; `C` = `{"kind":"project","id":"<doc id>"}`; ids are ONE worked example — use your own.

WHILE THEY WATCH — fill ONE section per call, the first right after the birth and the open, with a short
chat line on what you're on between calls; never the whole doc in one call. Why: the doc is usually open
on their screen as you work, and a call streams nothing — its text shows only once the whole call is
generated, so a one-call doc is a long blank page, then a wall of text.
Anything you will write only after going to get it (a section to research, a table to build, notes to pull), on ANY
road: FIRST plant a pending block where it will land, its intent = what comes (`Standup topics — checking Slack and
last week's notes`), then `replace` it with the content — they see the plan in place, then watch it fill.

OPEN THE DOC RIGHT AFTER ITS BIRTH — a doc born through `batch` is on nobody's screen. The birth
ack's trailer hands you its link (this server minted the viewer: `created.bound:true`; a `bound:false`
ack carries a notice and no link). When your Artifact tool has an `open` action, opening that link is
your very next call, before any fill: `Artifact( action = "open", url = "<the trailer's link>" )`.
No `open` action, or no Artifact tool: your very next message starts with the link, once, before any fill (not
again in the closing line). Never assume the doc is already open unless its trailer says so. Skip the open
(or the link) and the person sees nothing — no card, no doc on their screen, only your claim that a
doc exists, which reads as broken.

INTERACTIONS
- A doc-shaped ask (even phrased as a question) → a doc, never the document in chat; a quick question → chat.
- Change only what was asked; every other word stays. Facts only from the doc, the user, a commenter.
- Refused call = nothing changed; it names `code` (+ `path`) and the fix → resend the whole corrected call;
  still unclear → `guide( items = ["refusal.<code>"] )`.
- Calls on things IN a doc (a tab, its contents, a comment, `batch`) carry `"container": C`; a call whose `ref` IS
  the doc (doc read, rename, `tabs` patch) carries none. Ids in full (IDS).
- The doc changes between and during your turns: bookmark = your last read's `rev` (none yet: last ack's);
  a later turn touching the doc starts `read( …, payload = {"kind":"view","sinceRev":<bookmark>} )` →
  changed blocks only; no read between your own writes; `guard_mismatch` / `find_none` = that block changed
  → their edit wins, never resend with `force`, say what you kept (`refusal.<code>`, topic.editing).
- Convention left open (°C/°F, currency, calendar vs fiscal year) → pick the asker's likely one, label units in
  headers/axes, name the assumption in the reply in half a sentence, offer to switch.

- Where you write (one voice everywhere — short, specific, plain):
  - Doc (its tabs): lead sentence = the answer, then the tables, charts, diagrams, short sections that carry it;
    a memo, plan or review reads top-down (lead + short sections); a reference tab (comparison, schedule,
    dataset, sources) = title, lead, the table or chart, next to no prose.
  - Chat reply = a line or two, no ids, tool words or doc text: after create → one short line (~12 words) in your own
    words: the title as a link (once in the reply) + what they can do now (edit inline, comment, share) — nothing
    else, no recap of the doc; e.g. `<Title> is up — edit or comment and I'll revise.` or `Here's <Title>; tweak it
    or drop comments.`; after edits → what changed.
  - Comment thread = the answer or the change made, fitted to its card (~40 characters a line, 20 words fill three;
    more when the answer needs it); the edit itself already shows in the doc.
  - First sentence of the doc and of each section = its point (decision, result, answer + its number or
    date), never "This document outlines…".
  - Sized to the ask (often title + lead + one table): every heading, table, list answers the ask's own words;
    a topic it didn't name (background, causes, next steps, related figures) → ≤ 1 sentence in the lead or
    under the table, never its own section/table/list; no intro, recap, "key takeaways", methodology; an
    as-of date and sources are not extras.
  - Specifics, not adjectives: numbers + units, names, dates; a missing fact = a one-line open question.
    Sentences < 25 words, paragraphs ≤ 3 sentences, plain words, bullets only for parallel items, no emoji,
    the user's language.

SHAPE THE CONTENT (build the structure the content has — don't describe it in sentences)
- YOUR READER is a person who looks before reading: a picture's layout (what sits where, what is grouped, which
  way the arrows run) lands at a glance; prose is read a word at a time with a handful of items held in mind, so
  a shape told in sentences — things tied to each other, items judged on several dimensions at once, change over
  time, order and dependency, parts of a whole — is rebuilt in the reader's head. You read a list and a picture
  alike, as text, and a list costs you less to write: what a missing picture costs, the reader pays, out of your
  sight. A comment reply is read in a narrow card beside the page that folds when it runs long. The work people
  hand each other usually carries its argument on an exhibit or two; the exhibits you can make here: a drawing,
  a chart, an image (a file you hold → upload → blob → embed: `topic.uploads`; a file's name says little about
  what it shows, and you can look at an image before you place it).
- WHAT PEOPLE CAN DO with each form: a pipe table is the form people work in — they add rows and columns, type
  in its cells, pick from dropdown chips, comment on a cell · `- [ ]` tasks — they tick them off; a ticked
  item's first paragraph shows struck through and dimmed: words meant to be read go in a paragraph under it, or
  the item stays unticked · a drawing or a mock-up (a widget) — read at a glance; they edit its label words in
  place and comment on its parts; nothing else they do in it is kept (a box ticked or a value typed there is
  gone on reload) · a chart drawn from rows — read at a glance; they hover a value, open its data, comment on a
  point; its numbers change only through its rows.
- Numbers with a shape — a quantity over periods (a dated run of changes to ONE quantity too: points on a
  timeline, not table rows), one measure across items, a low–high range per period or item, parts of a whole;
  five or more values → a CHART, no companion table of the same values, ONE timeline start → now (per-year
  sections only when the ask compares years). Mark by shape: level over time → line; a range, or a band with two
  edges → ONE point (the middle) + whisker [low, high] per x, never floating bars or a one-edge line; several
  series at one x → side by side, stacked only when they sum to a whole; items × periods → grouped bars or a line
  per item; signed changes → bars about zero under the level. `guide( items = ["topic.charts"] )` once, then
  PLAN it (next bullet) and HAND-ROLL it (a `claude.Visualize` module that draws its own svg from `sources`),
  one `batch` (widget + embed). THEN LOOK → a chart is written without seeing its render, and a widget write's
  reply carries no picture: a screenshot `read` of the widget, its own call (`topic.charts`, LOOKING spells it),
  returns the chart as the page draws it. No picture back = go on without it, and never say you looked at a
  picture you did not see.
- Plan before you draw. Before a chart's first widget write, put a short brief in words (your working lines, not
  the doc): the reader; the decision they are making; the finding as ONE sentence with its number; the kind of
  chart the best practitioner in that reader's field would draw for it (some questions have a known answer: what
  moved a total from one value to another is a bridge, drawn by hand as a waterfall from the rows), and where the
  obvious chart (the table's columns as they come) falls short of that; the rows regrouped as that chart needs.
  Put the brief through the review below before you draw. Why first: the kind of chart is chosen before any look,
  and a look at your own finished chart mostly ends in keeping it; a brief has nothing to defend yet. A small
  plain chart takes a line or two. What no brief skips is the question of what that practitioner would draw: the
  answer is usually known and simply not asked for.
- Adversarial review. You are likely biased toward what you just wrote. When a brief, a visual or a long passage
  is done, get a fresh-eyes review before you move on: a sub-agent if you can start one (it can make the look
  too), otherwise reread it as a demanding outsider would. A visual: look at it rendered (THEN LOOK, above).
  Correct is not enough: is it the right visual for the reader's decision, and does it make its point at a
  glance, at the standard of highly professional work, so that a demanding expert would hand it over as it
  stands? If not, change it until they would, which may mean a different kind of chart, not only a cleaner one.
  Text: is it longer than the reader needs, and is the document's structure right? Revise what the review
  finds; what the reader needs stays in.
- Items × attributes of DIFFERENT kinds (price, size, owner, date, status, link: options, line items, people +
  roles; events/releases only when no one quantity is tracked), or a handful of values to look up → a pipe
  TABLE: row per item, column per attribute compared, units in the header, sorted by what readers scan for
  (dated rows newest first); a LOG of dated events already past (releases shipped, incidents, a changelog) = ONE
  such table, date · item · one line, newest first — never per-area sections or prose. Not rows: a PLAN's dates
  (milestones ahead, by team or workstream, what gates what) = a drawn timeline, and items placed on two axes
  (each scored on impact and effort, risk and value) = a 2x2 — the next bullet: the order and the position are
  the point, and rows hide them; columns that are one measure at several dates/groups → a chart instead.
- Steps or stages in a straight run read best as a numbered list the reader can reorder; those that branch, loop,
  run side by side or change hands (a request/approval flow, states + transitions, a call sequence), an architecture (components +
  what calls what), a reporting tree, items placed on two axes (impact × effort, risk × value) = a 2x2, pillars,
  a driver tree, a market map, a FUNNEL (stage counts + the drop-off between), a ROADMAP with phases + gates
  (criteria marked on the line), a TIMELINE of milestones ahead (a lane per team or workstream, the gate marked)
  → a DIAGRAM — those three too, never a table + a list (a date or a score on every item does not make it a
  table): a widget node whose module returns SVG (labels edited in place) → `guide( items = ["topic.diagram"] )` once (a funnel's counts = data →
  `"topic.charts"` too, in its own call — the largest topic; some clients cut a long result), then one `batch`
  (widget + embed); many siblings a level → left to right, deep chain → top
  down; one sentence of reading under it.
- A formula → a ```latex code block of bare TeX (no `$`): a display formula, never inline; in a sentence plain text
  (× not `\times`). CSV the reader copies out or edits as text (a comma-separated sample) → a ```csv code block,
  shown as a read-only grid over that editable text; a table people edit in place or compare stays a pipe table, a
  series a chart. Markdown shown as a rendered exhibit (a changelog, a template) → a ```markdown code block; the
  doc's own text is never wrapped in one (`"as":"markdown"` is only how content is sent).
- Two or three numbers, one fact, a yes/no → a sentence. A picture or file the user gave → the upload, placed
  where discussed: `guide( items = ["topic.uploads"] )`.
- Measure once: a number readers compare lives in a table XOR a chart, once in the doc; ≤ 6 rows of prices,
  specs or totals with no time axis = a table, no chart. A column you can't fill → left out, no "n/a".
- Looked-up facts: open (fetch) the pages you take numbers or dates from — a search snippet is not a source —
  and cite them IN THE DOC: `[source](url)` beside the table or a short Sources list (or tab) of pages actually
  opened, + an as-of date chip; every name of a person, product, filing or document taken from a source page
  links to it, even with the same URL each (in a table the name cell carries the link; under a diagram, the
  table/list of those names); a company period = fiscal label + calendar months once ("fiscal Q2 FY26 (Jan–Mar
  2026)"). Nothing to look things up with → say so in one line, label memory figures "approximate", never as sourced.

CREATE A DOC (ex.1: ONE `batch` births the doc — FIRST call of the turn, before any research or `guide`; ex.2 fills it)
- `container` + `batch` = the two top-level keys of ONE call, `{"container":{…},"batch":[…]}`; no `container` →
  refused. A NEW doc: `container.create` = `{"name", "doc":{"markdown", "blocks"?}}` and `batch` = `[]` (ex.1) — the
  door makes the tab (`f`), its prose body (`n`) and the pointer between them; the ack's `lids` hands you both ids.
  More tabs in that birth, or a tab on an EXISTING doc (`container` = `C`) = members you spell → topic.tabs.
- Member keys: `verb`, `object` (create) or `ref` (update/read/delete), `engine`?, `payload`, `$lid`? — no
  others: prose ops `{"op":…}` go INSIDE an update member's `payload.ops`, never as members; content =
  `source.from` (`{"kind":"inline","content":…}`), never `source.content`.
- Byline under the title = EXACTLY `<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>` (as-of date chip · author = the
  user): no status word, sources, scope or caveats on that line (a status people change = a dropdown column of
  a tracker table, never a byline word); no chip for an owner or date the user didn't give (CHIPS).
- Outline = that first markdown, final, open for the user before any research: title, byline (+ a lead if the ask
  gives one), then ONE pending block per section the ask needs — `<?claude block sN?>` +
  `"sN":{"type":"pending","intent":"Risks: what could slip and the fallback"}` in `blocks` (ex.1: the heading, then
  plain words for what comes or what you will look up; a section whose content has a shape NAMES its picture —
  `"intent":"Rollout: a drawn timeline of the milestones by team"` — the plan that names a drawing gets one; a drawing takes longer to write than prose and its pending block shows the reader it is coming, so it can be filled after the prose sections; an overview can name one too: `"intent":"At a glance: a diagram of how the parts fit together"`), no `##` lines: each heading arrives with its fill; a one-table or one-chart answer = title, byline, lead, that block, no sections; a short memo or note =
  title + its few paragraphs, whole, no sections/tables/tasks unless asked.
- Before the first fill, look over the sections you planted: one whose content has a SHAPE — a branching flow, an
  architecture, a hierarchy, a timeline of milestones, items on two axes, a funnel; or five or more numbers that run over time or compare items —
  is filled with a DRAWING, whatever its intent said: the outline planted before this guide is a best first pass, not a
  promise (a better structure found while writing is taken; a picture that helps where the outline named none is drawn), and a shape set as rows makes the reader rebuild it in their head. OPEN ITS TOPIC NOW —
  `guide( items = ["topic.diagram"] )` (numbers: `["topic.charts"]`, in its own call) — drawing is taught only there; that
  section's fill = the topic's one `batch` (widget + embed), the embed under its `## <heading>` (SHAPE THE
  CONTENT says which shape is which).
- The fill (ex.2) = one `update` on `lids.n` PER SECTION, the first right after the open, while they watch (the prose sections first, in reading order; the pictures after them): a
  `replace` of its pending block (id off `n`'s ack) with `## <heading>` + the body, `"as":"markdown"`, no read,
  no new sections: paragraphs, bullets, `1.` lists (sub-points indented 4 spaces), `- [ ]` tasks, pipe tables,
  `[text](url)` links, what you looked up — or the section's drawing (above); a picture or file the user gave → `guide( items = ["topic.uploads"] )` first (a CSV to chart is uploaded and
  cited by the chart, never retyped as rows) — `ref` is the doc NODE `{"object":"node","id":"<lids.n>"}`, never a block id; the pending block's id goes in `target.ids`; `payload` is always the cell `{"ops":[…]}` (ex.2).
- Birth is light: the person sees nothing until the birth `batch` returns with the link — an outline returns
  in seconds, a whole doc several times slower and all at once; every later call renders live into the open doc.
- A doc = ONE concise tab, cited links in a Sources section at its end; a further tab only for material with its
  own bulk or reasoning (working notes, cross-checks, raw data, many compared sources). The ask IS a set of
  tabs (one per call, partner, day) → all born in the birth batch, beside `container.create.doc`: each extra tab = three
  members (topic.tabs ex.1: `$lid:f2` a file whose value is just its `birthName`, `$lid:n2` a prose node whose `parent`
  is `$lid:f2`, the update pointing `f2` at `n2`) + ONE last member placing them all, main tab (`$lid:f`) first:
  `{"verb":"update","ref":{"object":"project","id":"$lid:p"},"payload":{"kind":"patch","patch":[{"op":"set","path":["tabs","$lid:f"],"value":{"name":"Plan","order":"a0"}},{"op":"set","path":["tabs","$lid:f2"],"value":{"name":"Sources","order":"a1"}}]}}`
  (`$lid:p` = the doc being born; a doc is a root — outside a batch its `update` carries `ref` alone, never a
  `container`); `guide( items = ["topic.tabs"] )` → tabs added later, nesting (raw data under Sources), tab chips.

EDIT A DOC (find it, read only what you need, change only what was asked)
```
read( ref = {"object":"project","id":"3f2a9c1e-5b7d-4e8a-9c21-7d4e5f6a8b90"} )
  → files:[{id:"afc001d0-ce07", name:"Tab 1", content:{kind:"node", id:"be1476b2-62c1", engine:"prose"}}] = tab id, the tab's body id + its engine
    (a file's own "engine":"json" is the file record's, not its content's); C = this doc from here on
read( ref = {"object":"node","id":"be1476b2-62c1"}, engine = "prose", container = C, payload = {"projection":"outline"} )
  → <doc rev='12'><paragraph id='mq2x81a0kfd.0' heading='1'>Q3 launch …</paragraph><paragraph id='.16' h='cddc588b'>Q3 ships …</paragraph><list id='.40' kind='bullet'><gap blocks='2'/></list><table id='.90'>…
update( ref = {"object":"node","id":"be1476b2-62c1"}, engine = "prose", container = C,
        payload = {"ops":[
          {"op":"replace","target":{"kind":"find","text":"500 weekly active teams"},
           "with":{"from":{"kind":"inline","content":"750 weekly active teams"},"as":"text"}},
          {"op":"insert","target":{"kind":"blocks","ids":["mq2x81a0kfd.90"]},"side":"after",
           "source":{"from":{"kind":"inline","content":"## Risks\n\n- GA slips if legal review runs long"},"as":"markdown"}} ]} )
```
- Before a delete or a move, table rows/columns, or bringing back text someone deleted (it lives in the doc's
  history — never retype from memory) → `guide( items = ["topic.editing"] )` FIRST; it prints those ops
  (`move`, `delete`, row ops, list kinds) — never guess an op's shape.
- Targets: quotable words → `{"kind":"find","text":"…"}`, no read (`"nth":2` when the phrase repeats) — quote the words AS THEY STAND in your last read or ack; a paraphrase of them draws find_none — re-read that block and quote again; a
  whole block → its full id off the outline; a `replace`/`delete` of a whole block carries, beside `"op"`,
  BOTH `"ifHash"` = its newest `h` AND `"ifRev"` = the `rev` of the READ that showed it (an ack's only for a
  block that ack wrote whole):
  `{"op":"replace","target":{"kind":"blocks","ids":["mq2x81a0kfd.16"]},"ifHash":"cddc588b","ifRev":12,"with":{…}}`,
  or `"force":true` (only when told to overwrite); bare → `missing_guard` (a pending block's fill needs none;
  find/chars targets need none unless they select blocks or cells). `insert` → `"source":{from, as}`, `replace` →
  `"with":{from, as}`; `from` = `{"kind":"inline","content":"…"}` always, never `source.content` or a bare string.
- `"as":"text"` re-words in place, keeping chips, breaks, formatting, comments; `"as":"markdown"` = a whole list,
  table or section, all items/rows re-sent, keeping only what it re-spells. `side`: `"before"` | `"after"` a block; `{"kind":"root"}` + `"end"` = end of
  the tab; `"end"` on a heading id = end of its section (ex.2). Several ops per call.
- Never pull a long doc whole: outline, then `payload = {"kind":"view","parentId":"mq2x81a0kfd.90"}` (one
  table/list in full) or `{"kind":"search","text":"weekly active"}`.
- `complete:false` = a partial read: repeat it with `next`'s keys added to its `payload` (no payload: `{"kind":"view"}`).
- The request says the person is in Suggesting mode, or the viewer context has `"suggesting":true` → every change
  is a suggestion, not a plain edit.
- Asked to suggest an edit or to reword what is there ("tighten", "improve"), in that mode, or a read shows
  `<ins s=…>` / `<del s=…>` (proposed, not yet accepted) → `guide( items = ["topic.suggestions"] )`.
- A `sinceRev` read whose root says `since='unavailable'` = the whole doc, not a delta: it replaces your copy.
  With view-only access a delta carries no `<gone/>`: a removed block born at or before your `sinceRev` brings
  the whole doc instead; one born after it is just absent from the delta → `sinceRev` = your latest read's `rev`,
  so every block you hold is covered.

COMMENTS (`"utterance"` objects under a tab's body; thread = its first comment)
- Comment on words (no read first):
  ```
  create( object = "utterance", container = C,
          payload = {"value":{"parent":{"object":"node","id":"<body id>","anchor":{"kind":"find","text":"<3–6 words exactly as in the doc>"}},
                     "body":"Which workspaces first?"}} )
  ```
  words occur twice → `"nth":2` in the anchor. Reply in a thread: same call,
  `"parent":{"object":"utterance","id":"<first comment id>"}`, no `anchor`. A note for collaborators on the
  whole tab: parent the body id, no `anchor`. Write `parent` before `body`, however long the body: a comment, reply or note without `parent` is refused. List threads:
  `query( object = "utterance", container = C, payload = {"under":{"object":"node","id":"<body id>"}} )`. Acting on
  comments, rows (`to:"claude"`, resolve, `actor.self`), paging, limits → `guide( items = ["topic.comments"] )` first.
- A comment SENT to you = its own user turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`; the doc id ends its
  `Artifact:` link; `Element path: f-<tab id>#<body id>/<block>…;thread=<root id>`. **Smart Campaign Composer: Assignment Summary**

The assignment is to build an end-to-end system where a marketer describes a campaign in natural language, and Claude turns that into a target audience and SMS and email messages. The marketer reviews and approves the output, and the system sends the messages and shows delivery status live. All recipients are fake users and all sending goes to a mock provider you write. The case is due within 7 days.

**Example brief:** Remind Istanbul users who added items to their cart but didn't buy in the last 30 days about a 30% discount, in a friendly, short tone.

**User flow**
1. **Audience:** Claude generates a segment rule from the brief, and the UI shows how many people it covers.
2. **Messages:** SMS and email content streams to the screen.
3. **Approval:** The marketer previews, edits if needed, and approves.
4. **Sending:** Messages go through a queue to the mock provider.
5. **Monitoring:** A dashboard shows delivery status.

**Functional requirements**
- **Audience:** Backend validates the LLM's segment rule. LLM output must never run directly as SQL. Users without channel consent must not receive messages.
- **Content:** SMS max 160 characters, email subject max 80. Personalization variables like `{{first_name}}` must be supported.
- **Sending:** Async queue, max 100 messages per second per channel. The same message must never go to the same person twice. You design the retry strategy.
- **Tracking:** Live delivery status, metrics, and health check endpoints.

**AI requirements**
- Claude's output must be structured (JSON) and validated on the backend.
- Tests must run without a real API key, using a mock LLM.

**Resources you build yourself**
- Seed data for several thousand fake users. You choose the fields (e.g., name, email, phone, city, purchase history, channel consent).
- A mock SMS/email provider that occasionally returns errors, delays, and 429 rate-limit responses, so retry and rate-limit logic can be tested.
- The Claude API key is read from `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in `.env`, with a `.env.example` committed to the repo.

**Tech:** Vue.js frontend, Go or PHP backend. Database, queue, and libraries are your choice.

**Deliverables**
- Git repository (GitHub or GitLab)
- `docker compose up` to start everything, including seed data and mock provider
- `make test` to run tests
- `README.md` with setup and architecture overview
- `DECISIONS.md` with key decisions and reasons
- `ai-sessions/` folder with your Claude session exports, with API keys and personal data removed

Scope note: they prefer a solid core flow over completing everything. Anything unfinished should be listed in the README.

**Bonus (optional):** scheduled sending, A/B variants, language-based content, CI pipeline.

**AI tool use:** Using Claude Code, Cursor, or similar is allowed and expected. You must understand and take ownership of the code. Session exports are reviewed to see how you approached the problem and verified AI output, not to score how much you used AI.

**Grading weights**
- LLM integration: 25%
- Architecture and decisions: 20%
- Backend reliability: 20%
- Frontend: 20%
- Tests and code quality: 15%

**Next step:** If the project looks good, there is a 30-minute review call to discuss your solution and decisions. Contact the organizer for questions or extra time.

input.content:
# Decisions

Key choices and why. Entries marked *proposed* are still open.

## Stack

| Area | Choice | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Backend | Go, stdlib `net/http` router (method + path patterns) | No framework needed; fewer dependencies to explain. |
| Database | PostgreSQL 17 via `pgx/v5`, hand-written SQL, embedded `.sql` migrations | Segment rules compile to parameterised SQL, so we want direct control of the queries. |
| Local/test DB | `embedded-postgres` when `DATABASE_URL` is unset; one migrated DB per test | `make test` runs with no Docker and no shared state between tests. |
| Queue | *Proposed:* Postgres table queue (`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` + leases) | Delivery rows are created in the same transaction as campaign approval, and a `UNIQUE (campaign_id, user_id, channel)` key makes double sends impossible at the DB level. No second datastore. Alternative considered: asynq + Redis (built-in retries and task-ID dedup, but a dual write between Postgres and Redis). |
| Rate limiting | `golang.org/x/time/rate`, one limiter per channel (100/s) | Single worker process, so an in-process token bucket is enough. |
| Realtime | Server-Sent Events, Postgres `LISTEN/NOTIFY` as the wake-up signal | One-way server → browser is all we need; works through plain HTTP. |
| LLM | Claude via the Messages API behind a small `Provider` interface; scripted fake for tests | Tests never touch the network; the real adapter is swapped in when `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is set. |
| LLM output | Forced tool use for JSON, then JSON Schema validation + a field/operator allowlist | The model never writes SQL; the backend owns query construction. |
| Metrics | `prometheus/client_golang` on `/metrics`, plus `/healthz` and `/readyz` | Standard, and the dashboard can read the same counters. |
| Frontend | Vue 3 + Vite + TypeScript, Tailwind v4 | Required Vue; Tailwind for speed. |
| Logging | `log/slog`, text locally, JSON in Compose | Stdlib, structured. |

**What the scaffold has:** a Go server with only a health endpoint, the environment config, and its test. There's also a Makefile, a Dockerfile, a Compose file (Postgres + server), [README.md](README.md), [DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md) with the proposed stack and reasons, `.env.example` and `ai-sessions/`. **What we can bring over from agents-platform** (it's our main base):
- **LLM layer:** the small provider interface, the retry with exponential backoff and jitter that respects `Retry-After`, the stream parser, and the scripted fake LLM. The fake gives `make test` its no-key mock LLM. It has no Claude adapter, so I'll write that one.
- **Validation:** the JSON Schema check, with errors the model can read and fix. It will check Claude's segment rule against a fixed list of allowed fields and operators before we build safe SQL from it.
- **Queue:** the Postgres-backed job pattern (workers claim rows with a lease and skip rows others hold, plus a heartbeat and a sweeper for stuck jobs). I'll adapt it into a smaller `deliveries` table.
- **Live updates:** the Server-Sent Events handler that can resume after a reconnect, and the Postgres listen/notify hub behind it. This fits both the streamed copy and the live delivery dashboard.
- **Database and tests:** the migration runner, the embedded Postgres fallback, and one fresh database per test. So `make test` needs neither Docker nor a key.
- **Plumbing:** the HTTP error helpers, the middleware, and the Compose healthcheck setup.
- **Not needed here:** the multi-agent orchestration, the opencode harness and the sandbox. We only need one Claude call for the audience rule and one streamed call for the messages.

**What we can bring over from other-project:**
- **Error handling:** the typed provider errors that decide retry or fail (429 and timeouts retry, permanent errors don't). This maps straight onto the mock provider.
- **Retries:** its backoff curve (wait grows with the square of the attempt number, capped) and its dead-letter handling for jobs that run out of retries.
- **Metrics:** Prometheus counters and histograms, since agents-platform has no metrics.
- **LLM output:** its forgiving JSON parsing, kept as a fallback layer.

Neither project has Vue code; both frontends are React, so only patterns carry over there. The live-status hook becomes a Vue composable, and the Tailwind + shadcn styling becomes shadcn-vue.

**The one decision that's yours: the queue.**
- **What I'd pick: a Postgres table.** Delivery rows are written in the same transaction as the approval. A unique key on campaign, user and channel makes a double send impossible at the database level.
- **The alternative: asynq + Redis from other-project.** Retries and deduplication come built in, but every approval then writes to both Postgres and Redis, and those two can get out of sync.

DECISIONS.md marks the queue as proposed until you decide.

input.content:
# AI sessions

Exports of the Claude Code sessions used to build this project, with API keys and personal data removed.
Each session has two files:

- `NN-name.md`: readable conversation. Tool calls and results are collapsed and truncated.
- `NN-name.jsonl`: the full conversation record (user and assistant turns, tool calls, tool results).

## How they are produced

1. Export the session from the Claude app (session menu → Export). This gives a zip.
2. Run the scrubber:

   ```bash
   make session IN=~/Downloads/session-export-<id>.zip NAME=01-setup-and-scaffold
   ```

The scrubber (`tools/sessionexport`) keeps only the main conversation. It drops subagent transcripts,
app metadata and internal request payloads. Then it:

- replaces the home directory with `~` and the OS username with `<user>`,
- replaces email addresses with `<email>` (commit-trailer and example domains are kept),
- removes the app's list of recently used local folders,
- applies extra `find => replace` rules from a gitignored `.scrub.local` file,
- refuses to write anything if a credential-shaped string or any private term is still present.

Exporting works and is now safe to share. I ran the new tool on a fresh export of this session and the output came out clean. To export a session from now on:
1. Export it from the session menu (Export), which saves a zip.

```bash
make session IN=~/Downloads/session-export-<id>.zip NAME=01-setup-and-scaffold
```

It writes two files into `ai-sessions/`: a readable `.md` with tool calls collapsed, and the full `.jsonl` record. If anything private survives, it writes nothing and reports only the line number and type of the problem, never the value.

What the tool does:
- **Keeps only the main conversation.** It drops the app's metadata, the internal request data and the survey agents' raw transcripts. The agents' final reports stay, since they're part of the main chat.

1	// Package store is the PostgreSQL data access layer. Every method that reads or
2	// writes team-owned data takes the caller's team ID and filters by it, so team
3	// isolation does not depend on handlers remembering to check ownership.
4	package store
5	
6	import (
7		"context"
8		"errors"
9	
10		"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"
11		"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgconn"
12		"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool"
13	)
14	
15	var (
16		ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")
17		// ErrConflict means a unique constraint was violated, e.g. a duplicate name.
18		ErrConflict = errors.New("already exists")
19		// ErrInUse means a row is still referenced, e.g. a tool used by an agent.
20		ErrInUse = errors.New("still in use")
21		// ErrUnknownTool means an agent refers to a tool name its team does not have.
22		ErrUnknownTool = errors.New("unknown tool")
23		// ErrUnknownMCPServer is the same for an MCP server name.
24		ErrUnknownMCPServer = errors.New("unknown MCP server")
25		// ErrUnknownAgent is the same for an agent an agent may call.
26		ErrUnknownAgent = errors.New("unknown agent")
27		// ErrForbidden means the user may see the resource but not do this.
28		ErrForbidden = errors.New("not allowed")
29	)
30	
31	type Store struct {
32		pool *pgxpool.Pool
33	}
34	
35	func New(pool *pgxpool.Pool) *Store {
36		return &Store{pool: pool}
37	}
38	
39	func (s *Store) Ping(ctx context.Context) error {
40		return s.pool.Ping(ctx)
41	}
42	
43	// mapErr turns driver errors into the package's sentinel errors so callers can
44	// use errors.Is without knowing about PostgreSQL error codes.
45	// deleteOne runs a DELETE meant to remove exactly one row; ErrNotFound if it
46	// removed none (the row does not exist, or belongs to another team).
47	func (s *Store) deleteOne(ctx context.Context, sql string, args ...any) error {
48		tag, err := s.pool.Exec(ctx, sql, args...)
49		if err != nil {
50			return mapErr(err)
51		}
52		if tag.RowsAffected() == 0 {
53			return ErrNotFound
54		}
55		return nil
56	}
57	
58	func mapErr(err error) error {
59		if err == nil {
60			return nil
61		}
62		if errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows) {
63			return ErrNotFound
64		}
65		var pgErr *pgconn.PgError
66		if errors.As(err, &pgErr) {
67			switch pgErr.Code {
68			case "23505": // unique_violation
69				return ErrConflict
70			case "23503": // foreign_key_violation
71				return ErrInUse
72			case "22P02": // invalid_text_representation, e.g. a malformed UUID
73				return ErrNotFound
74			}
75		}
76		return err
77	}

2	//
3	// It uses TEST_DATABASE_URL when set (any database on a server where the user
4	// may create databases). Otherwise it starts an embedded PostgreSQL once per
5	// test binary, so `go test ./...` works without installing anything.
6	package testdb
7	
8	import (
9		"context"
10		"crypto/rand"
11		"encoding/hex"
12		"fmt"
13		"io"
14		"net"
15		"net/url"
16		"os"
17		"path/filepath"
18		"sync"
19		"testing"
20	
21		embeddedpostgres "github.com/fergusstrange/embedded-postgres"
22		"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"
23		"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool"
24	
25		"github.com/m<user>/agents-platform/internal/store"
26	)
27	
28	var (
29		mu        sync.Mutex
30		serverURL string
31		stopPG    func()
32	)
33	
34	// Main runs the tests and stops the embedded server afterwards, if one was
35	// started. Use it from TestMain: os.Exit(testdb.Main(m)).
36	func Main(m *testing.M) int {
37		code := m.Run()
38		mu.Lock()
39		defer mu.Unlock()
40		if stopPG != nil {
41			stopPG()
42		}
43		return code
44	}
45	
46	// New creates an empty, migrated database for this test and drops it when the
47	// test ends.
48	func New(t *testing.T) *pgxpool.Pool {
49		t.Helper()
50		ctx := context.Background()
51		base, err := server()
52		if err != nil {
53			t.Fatalf("test database server: %v", err)
54		}
55	
56		name := "test_" + randomHex(6)
57		if err := adminExec(ctx, base, "CREATE DATABASE "+name); err != nil {
58			t.Fatalf("create test database: %v", err)
59		}
60		pool, err := pgxpool.New(ctx, withDatabase(base, name))
61		if err != nil {
62			t.Fatalf("connect test database: %v", err)
63		}
64		t.Cleanup(func() {
65			pool.Close()
66			adminExec(ctx, base, "DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS "+name+" WITH (FORCE)")
67		})
68		if err := store.Migrate(ctx, pool); err != nil {
69			t.Fatalf("migrate test database: %v", err)
70		}
71		return pool
72	}
73	
74	func server() (string, error) {
75		mu.Lock()
76		defer mu.Unlock()
77		if serverURL != "" {
78			return serverURL, nil
79		}
80		if u := os.Getenv("TEST_DATABASE_URL"); u != "" {
81			serverURL = u
82			return u, nil
83		}
84	
85		port, err := freePort()
86		if err != nil {
87			return "", err
88		}
89		dir, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "agents-testpg-")
90		if err != nil {
91			return "", err
92		}
93		password := randomHex(12)
94		pg := embeddedpostgres.NewDatabase(embeddedpostgres.DefaultConfig().
95			Version(embeddedpostgres.V17).
96			Port(uint32(port)).
97			Username("postgres").
98			Password(password).
99			Database("postgres").
100			RuntimePath(filepath.Join(dir, "runtime")).
101			DataPath(filepath.Join(dir, "data")).
102			BinariesPath(filepath.Join(dir, "bin")).
103			Logger(io.Discard))
104		if err := pg.Start(); err != nil {
105			os.RemoveAll(dir)
106			return "", fmt.Errorf("start embedded postgres: %w", err)
107		}
108		stopPG = func() {
109			pg.Stop()
110			os.RemoveAll(dir)
111		}
112		serverURL = fmt.Sprintf("postgres://postgres:%s@localhost:%d/postgres?sslmode=disable", password, port)
113		return serverURL, nil
114	}
115	
116	func adminExec(ctx context.Context, base, sql string) error {
117		conn, err := pgx.Connect(ctx, base)
118		if err != nil {
119			return err
120		}
121		defer conn.Close(ctx)
122		_, err = conn.Exec(ctx, sql)
123		return err
124	}
125	
126	func withDatabase(base, name string) string {
127		u, err := url.Parse(base)
128		if err != nil {
129			return base
130		}
131		u.Path = "/" + name
132		return u.String()
133	}
134	
135	func freePort() (int, error) {
136		l, err := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0")
137		if err != nil {
138			return 0, err
139		}
140		defer l.Close()
141		return l.Addr().(*net.TCPAddr).Port, nil
142	}
143	
144	func randomHex(n int) string {
145		b := make([]byte, n)
146		rand.Read(b)
147		return hex.EncodeToString(b)
148	}

13	
14	type errorBody struct {
15		Error struct {
16			Code    string `json:"code"`
17			Message string `json:"message"`
18		} `json:"error"`
19	}
20	
21	func writeJSON(w http.ResponseWriter, status int, v any) {
22		w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
23		w.WriteHeader(status)
24		json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v)
25	}
26	
27	func writeError(w http.ResponseWriter, status int, code, message string) {
28		var body errorBody
29		body.Error.Code = code
30		body.Error.Message = message
31		writeJSON(w, status, body)
32	}

34	// decodeJSON reads a single JSON object into v and rejects unknown fields, so
35	// typos in a request do not get silently ignored.
36	func decodeJSON(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request, v any) bool {
37		dec := json.NewDecoder(http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, maxBodyBytes))
38		dec.DisallowUnknownFields()
39		err := dec.Decode(v)
40		if err == nil && !errors.Is(dec.Decode(&struct{}{}), io.EOF) {
41			err = errors.New("unexpected data after the object")
42		}
43		if err != nil {
44			writeError(w, http.StatusBadRequest, "invalid_request", "invalid JSON body: "+err.Error())
45			return false
46		}
47		return true
48	}

50	// storeError maps store errors to HTTP responses. Another team's resource is
51	// reported as not found, so its existence is not revealed.
52	func (s *Server) storeError(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request, err error, what string) {
53		switch {
54		case errors.Is(err, store.ErrNotFound):
55			writeError(w, http.StatusNotFound, "not_found", what+" not found")
56		case errors.Is(err, store.ErrConflict):
57			writeError(w, http.StatusConflict, "conflict", "a "+what+" with this name already exists")
58		case errors.Is(err, store.ErrInUse):
59			writeError(w, http.StatusConflict, "in_use", what+" is still used by an agent")
60		case errors.Is(err, store.ErrUnknownTool), errors.Is(err, store.ErrUnknownMCPServer), errors.Is(err, store.ErrUnknownAgent):
61			writeError(w, http.StatusBadRequest, "invalid_request", err.Error())
62		default:
63			s.internalError(w, r, err)
64		}
65	}

67	// internalError logs an unexpected error and answers 500 without details.
68	func (s *Server) internalError(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request, err error) {
69		s.log.Error("request failed", "method", r.Method, "path", r.URL.Path, "error", err)
70		writeError(w, http.StatusInternalServerError, "internal", "internal error")
71	}

115		t.ResponseHeaderTimeout = headerTimeout

119	// requestError wraps a failed HTTP call. A provider that did not start

121	// streamed yet.
122	func requestError(ctx context.Context, provider string, err error) error {
123		if cause := context.Cause(ctx); cause != nil {
124			return cause
125		}

127		if errors.As(err, &ne) && ne.Timeout() {
128			return &StatusError{Provider: provider, StatusCode: http.StatusGatewayTimeout,

150	// a provider ever echoes it.
151	func cleanMessage(msg, apiKey string) string {
152		msg = strings.TrimSpace(msg)
153		if apiKey != "" {
154			msg = strings.ReplaceAll(msg, apiKey, "***")
155		}

163	func parseRetryAfter(v string) time.Duration {
164		v = strings.TrimSpace(v)
165		if v == "" {
166			return 0
167		}
168		if d, err := time.ParseDuration(v + "s"); err == nil && d >= 0 {
169			return d
170		}
171		if t, err := time.Parse(time.RFC1123, v); err == nil {
172			return max(time.Until(t), 0)
173		}
174		return 0
175	}

131	// handleRunEvents streams a run's events with server-sent events. It first
132	// replays stored events after Last-Event-ID (set by the browser when it
133	// reconnects), then waits for new ones. Stored events and live ones come from
134	// the same query, so nothing falls in between.
135	func (s *Server) handleRunEvents(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
136		ctx := r.Context()
137		teamID := currentUser(r).TeamID
138		run, err := s.store.GetRun(ctx, teamID, r.PathValue("id"))
139		if err != nil {
140			s.storeError(w, r, err, "run")
141			return
142		}
143		after, _ := strconv.ParseInt(r.Header.Get("Last-Event-ID"), 10, 64)
144		if v := r.URL.Query().Get("after"); v != "" {
145			after, _ = strconv.ParseInt(v, 10, 64)
146		}
147	
148		// Subscribe before the first query, so an event stored in between still
149		// rings the bell.
150		sub := s.hub.Subscribe(run.ID)
151		defer s.hub.Unsubscribe(sub)
152	
153		rc := http.NewResponseController(w)
154		h := w.Header()
155		h.Set("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
156		h.Set("Cache-Control", "no-cache")
157		h.Set("X-Accel-Buffering", "no") // tell proxies not to buffer
158		w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
159		io.WriteString(w, "retry: 2000\n\n")
160		rc.Flush()
161	
162		keepAlive := time.NewTicker(15 * time.Second)
163		defer keepAlive.Stop()
164		for {
165			events, err := s.store.Events(ctx, run.ID, after)
166			if err != nil {
167				return
168			}
169			for _, ev := range events {
170				data, _ := json.Marshal(ev)
171				fmt.Fprintf(w, "id: %d\nevent: %s\ndata: %s\n\n", ev.Seq, ev.Type, data)
172				after = ev.Seq
173			}
174			rc.Flush()
175			// A run with follow-ups has a run_finished per turn, so the stream ends
176			// only when the run is finished now. "end" tells the browser not to
177			// reconnect.
178			if len(events) == 0 || events[len(events)-1].Type == "run_finished" {
179				if cur, err := s.store.GetRun(ctx, teamID, run.ID); err != nil || cur.Finished() {
180					io.WriteString(w, "event: end\ndata: {}\n\n")
181					rc.Flush()
182					return
183				}
184			}
185	
186		wait:
187			for {
188				select {
189				case <-ctx.Done():
190					return
191				case <-s.closing:
192					return
193				case <-keepAlive.C:
194					io.WriteString(w, ": keep-alive\n\n")
195					rc.Flush()
196					break wait // also re-reads, in case a doorbell was missed
197				case sig := <-sub.C:
198					if sig.Delta == "" {
199						break wait
200					}
201					data, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]string{"text": sig.Delta})
202					fmt.Fprintf(w, "event: model_delta\ndata: %s\n\n", data)
203					rc.Flush()
204				}
205			}
206		}
207	}

75	// addEvent appends an event inside tx and notifies listeners when tx commits.
76	// Taking the next seq from the run row locks it, so concurrent writers (the
77	// worker and an approval handler on another replica) get distinct numbers.
78	func addEvent(ctx context.Context, tx pgx.Tx, runID, typ string, data any) error {
79		b, err := json.Marshal(data)
80		if err != nil {
81			return err
82		}
83		if _, err := tx.Exec(ctx, `
84			WITH s AS (UPDATE runs SET event_seq = event_seq + 1 WHERE id = $1 RETURNING event_seq)
85			INSERT INTO run_events (run_id, seq, type, data) SELECT $1, event_seq, $2, $3 FROM s`,
86			runID, typ, b); err != nil {
87			return mapErr(err)
88		}
89		payload, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]string{"run": runID})
90		_, err = tx.Exec(ctx, `SELECT pg_notify($1, $2)`, NotifyChannel, string(payload))
91		return mapErr(err)

122				return nil, mapErr(err)
123			}
124			events = append(events, e)
125		}

# Building LLM-Powered Applications with Claude

This skill helps you build LLM-powered applications with Claude. Choose the right surface based on your needs, detect the project language, then read the relevant language-specific documentation.

## Before You Start

Scan the target file (or, if no target file, the prompt and project) for non-Anthropic provider markers - `import openai`, `from openai`, `langchain_openai`, `OpenAI(`, `gpt-4`, `gpt-5`, file names like `agent-openai.py` or `*-generic.py`, or any explicit instruction to keep the code provider-neutral. If you find any, stop and tell the user that this skill produces Claude/Anthropic SDK code; ask whether they want to switch the file to Claude or want a non-Claude implementation. Do not edit a non-Anthropic file with Anthropic SDK calls. (Exception: the `prompt-audit` subcommand is non-interactive and does not stop here - it records non-Anthropic provider markers in its report's stated assumptions and never proposes switching a non-Anthropic file to the Anthropic SDK.)

## Output Requirement

When the user asks you to add, modify, or implement a Claude feature, your code must call Claude through one of:

1. **The official Anthropic SDK** for the project's language (`anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai/sdk`, `com.anthropic.*`, etc.). This is the default whenever a supported SDK exists for the project.
2. **Raw HTTP** (`curl`, `requests`, `fetch`, `httpx`, etc.) - only when the user explicitly asks for cURL/REST/raw HTTP, the project is a shell/cURL project, or the language has no official SDK.

Never mix the two - don't reach for `requests`/`fetch` in a Python or TypeScript project just because it feels lighter. Never fall back to OpenAI-compatible shims.

**Never guess SDK usage.** Function names, class names, namespaces, method signatures, and import paths must come from explicit documentation - either the `{lang}/` files in this skill or the official SDK repositories or documentation links listed in `shared/live-sources.md`. If the binding you need is not explicitly documented in the skill files, fetch the relevant SDK repo from `shared/live-sources.md` before writing code. Do not infer Ruby/Java/Go/PHP/C# APIs from cURL shapes or from another language's SDK.

If you cannot call WebFetch yet and ToolSearch is among your tools, call ToolSearch with `select:WebFetch` first; of the tools it loads, call only the one named exactly `WebFetch`.

**If fetching or repository access fails** (network restricted, timeouts, clone blocked): do not keep retrying - write code from the patterns and namespace/package tables in the `{lang}/` file, run the compiler or interpreter on it, and iterate on the error output. For statically-typed SDKs (C#, Java, Go) a compile-fix loop against local errors reaches working code faster than blocked network research.

## Defaults

Unless the user requests otherwise:

For the Claude model version, please use Claude Opus 5.5, which you can access via the exact model string `claude-opus-5-5`. Please default to using adaptive thinking (`thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`) for anything remotely complicated. And finally, please default to streaming for any request that may involve long input, long output, or high `max_tokens` - it prevents hitting request timeouts. Use the SDK's `.get_final_message()` / `.finalMessage()` helper to get the complete response if you don't need to handle individual stream events. When a streaming request defines user-defined (client) tools, set `eager_input_streaming: true` on each of those tools so large tool inputs (file contents, code, documents) stream as they are generated instead of arriving in one burst after the server finishes buffering them; the client then owns validation: the SDKs' tolerant parsers can return a silently truncated input instead of raising, so validate each parsed tool input against its schema before running it (the typed runner helpers such as `betaZodTool` / typed `@beta_tool` do this; `betaTool()` JSON-Schema tools and manual loops must validate themselves), treat a failure like invalid JSON (`INVALID_JSON` error `tool_result` when you hold the block, re-issue otherwise), check `max_tokens` / `refusal` stop reasons before running tools, and catch only the SDK's JSON error, never its typed API errors - pattern in `shared/tool-use-concepts.md` -> Eager input streaming. Leave it off for non-streaming requests, for server tools, and when the request goes through a proxy or an older Bedrock model deployment that rejects the field.

## Warning: API Drift - Your Training Prior May Be Stale

Several common Claude API shapes changed in 2025-2026. If you recall a pattern from training, verify it against the `{lang}/` files in this skill before writing - the rows below are the most frequent drift points:

| Area | Stale prior | Current API |
|---|---|---|
| Extended thinking | `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}` | On Claude 4.6+ models: `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`. `budget_tokens` is deprecated on Opus 4.6 / Sonnet 4.6 and **rejected with a 400** on Fable 5/5.1/5.2 / Sonnet 5.5 / Sonnet 5 / Opus 5.5 / 5 / 4.8 / 4.7. Pre-4.6 models still use `budget_tokens`. |
| Web search / web fetch tool type | `web_search_20250305`, `web_fetch_20250910` | `web_search_20260209`, `web_fetch_20260209` (dynamic filtering) on Fable and Mythos models, Opus 5.5/5/4.8/4.7/4.6, Sonnet 5.5, Sonnet 5, and Sonnet 4.6. Older models keep the basic variants; on Vertex AI only basic `web_search_20250305` is available (web fetch is not on Vertex) - see the Server Tools QR below. |
| PHP parameter names | snake_case wire names as named args (`max_tokens`) | Top-level named args are camelCase (`maxTokens`). Nested array keys vary by feature (e.g. `'taskBudget'`, `'skillID'`, `'mcp_server_name'`) - copy the exact key from the documented example; do not bulk-convert. |

## Which Surface Should I Use?

> **Start simple.** Default to the simplest tier that meets your needs. Single API calls and workflows handle most use cases - only reach for agents when the task genuinely requires open-ended, model-driven exploration, or the user asks for an agent. "Simplest" means the least code you own: for an agent, that is usually Managed Agents (no harness to host, no state files, no scheduler).

| Use Case                                        | Tier            | Recommended Surface       | Why                                                          |
| ----------------------------------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Classification, summarization, extraction, Q&A  | Single LLM call | **Claude API**            | One request, one response                                    |
| Batch processing or embeddings                  | Single LLM call | **Claude API**            | Specialized endpoints                                        |
| Multi-step pipelines with code-controlled logic | Workflow        | **Claude API + tool use** | You orchestrate the loop                                     |
| Agent whose loop and compute the user hosts | Agent | **Claude API + tool use** | Maximum flexibility |
| Any other agent | Agent | **Managed Agents** | Anthropic runs the loop and hosts the tool-execution sandbox |
| Persisted, versioned agent configs              | Agent           | **Managed Agents**        | Agents are stored objects; sessions pin to a version         |
| Long-running multi-turn agent with file mounts  | Agent           | **Managed Agents**        | Per-session containers, SSE event stream, Skills + MCP       |
| Agent that runs on a schedule (cron, "every night") | Agent       | **Managed Agents** - scheduled deployments | Deployments fire sessions autonomously; no client-side scheduler |
| One deliverable that must meet a quality bar ("until it's right") | Agent | **Managed Agents** - outcomes | A separate grader iterates the agent against your rubric until it passes |
| Agent work split across several agents | Agent | **Managed Agents** - dynamic workflows | Many agents in phases |

> **Agents default to Managed Agents.** When the user asks for an agent, or for something whose model chooses its own tool calls over several turns (an assistant or bot with tools counts, a code-driven workflow doesn't), build on Managed Agents without asking first: "simple", a new project, a command-line tool or "the Claude API" says nothing about who hosts it. Tell them briefly that Anthropic hosts the agent loop and the container where its tools run, that it's in beta, bills session runtime on top of tokens and keeps session history until deleted, and that you can use the Messages API instead if they'd rather host it. Use Claude API + tool use instead only when the user says they want just a harness or will host the loop and compute themselves; names the Messages API or Tool Runner; has said no to Managed Agents; needs Zero Data Retention or HIPAA BAA coverage (not currently eligible); is on a platform without Managed Agents; or already runs the project's agent loop on the Messages API. The user's own tools or compute alone don't change the default: use custom tools, MCP or a `self_hosted` environment. On the Messages API, use the tool runner (`shared/tool-use-concepts.md`) or the manual loop.

> **Cloud-provider access.** **Claude Platform on AWS** is Anthropic-operated with same-day API parity - see `shared/claude-platform-on-aws.md` for client setup. **Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed)** is Anthropic-operated too (`shared/google-cloud-anthropic-managed.md`); elsewhere in this skill, "Google Cloud" and "Vertex" as platform names mean Google's Vertex AI. If a user says only "Google Cloud" and the code doesn't settle it, ask which they use. For availability on each of these, **Amazon Bedrock**, and **Microsoft Foundry**, see `shared/platform-availability.md` - that table is the single source of truth in this skill; do not infer availability from anywhere else.

### Building an Agent: Four Approaches

There are four ways to build an agent. Two independent questions separate them: **who supplies the harness** (the agent loop + context management) and **who supplies the deployment** (the infra the agent runs on).

| # | Approach | You write | Harness & deployment | Tools available | Use when |
|---|----------|-----------|----------------------|-----------------|----------|
| 1 | **Claude API - manual loop** | The `while stop_reason == "tool_use"` loop yourself | You build the harness; you host | Only tools you define | You want to own the *entire* loop - no beta dependency, or a control flow the Tool Runner's per-turn hooks don't fit |
| 2 | **Claude API - Tool Runner** (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner` + `@beta_tool` / `betaZodTool`) | Just the tool functions | SDK supplies the loop (**harness only**); you host | Only tools you define | You host the agent and don't want to write the loop. Per-turn hooks still give you approval gates, error interception, result modification (e.g. `cache_control`), retries, streaming, and compaction |
| 3 | **Managed Agents** (REST, beta) | Agent config + your tool results | Anthropic supplies the harness **and** hosts a per-session sandbox (**harness + deployment**) | Anthropic-hosted sandbox (bash, files, code exec) + Skills/MCP + your tools | Default: Anthropic runs the loop *and* hosts the per-session workspace; persisted/versioned configs; long-running sessions |
| 4 | **Claude Agent SDK** - *separate product* (`claude-agent-sdk` / `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`) | A prompt + options | SDK supplies the Claude Code harness + built-in tools (**harness only**); you host | Built-in Read/Write/Edit/Bash/Glob/Grep/WebSearch/WebFetch + MCP + subagents | You want a batteries-included coding/filesystem agent running on your own infra |

> **Tool Runner != Claude Agent SDK.** These sound alike but are different packages:
> - **Tool Runner** is part of the regular Anthropic API SDK (`anthropic` / `@anthropic-ai/sdk`), reached via `client.beta.messages.tool_runner`. It automates the request -> execute -> loop cycle *for tools you define*. No built-in tools, no filesystem access, no sandbox - you supply every tool and host the compute. It is option 2 above, a thin helper over `POST /v1/messages`.
> - **Claude Agent SDK** (`claude-agent-sdk` / `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`) is Claude Code packaged as a library. It ships built-in tools (file read/write/edit, bash, grep, web search), the full agent loop, context management, hooks, subagents, permissions, and sessions. You call `query(prompt, options)` and it drives everything.
>
> Both are **harness-only - you host and deploy them.** The difference is scope of harness: the Tool Runner loops over tools *you* define (with per-turn hooks for approval, interception, result modification, and retries - but no built-in tools); the Agent SDK is the full Claude Code harness with built-in tools. Neither provides managed deployment - that's what **Managed Agents (CMA)** adds (Anthropic hosts the loop and a per-session sandbox).
>
> **This skill covers the Claude API and Managed Agents (options 1-3); it does not generate Claude Agent SDK code.** If the user actually wants the Claude Agent SDK, point them to its docs (`code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk`) - don't substitute the API Tool Runner for it, or vice-versa.

### Should I Build an Agent?

Unless the request already describes an agent, check all four criteria first:

- **Complexity** - Is the task multi-step and hard to fully specify in advance? (e.g., "turn this design doc into a PR" vs. "extract the title from this PDF")
- **Value** - Does the outcome justify higher cost and latency?
- **Viability** - Is Claude capable at this task type?
- **Cost of error** - Can errors be caught and recovered from? (tests, review, rollback)

If the answer is "no" to any of these, stay at a simpler tier (single call or workflow).

## Architecture

Everything goes through `POST /v1/messages`. Tools and output constraints are features of this single endpoint - not separate APIs.

**User-defined tools** - You define tools (via decorators, Zod schemas, or raw JSON), and the SDK's tool runner handles calling the API, executing your functions, and looping until Claude is done. For full control, you can write the loop manually.

**Server-side tools** - Anthropic-hosted tools that run on Anthropic's infrastructure. Code execution is fully server-side (declare it in `tools`, Claude runs code automatically). Computer use can be server-hosted or self-hosted.

**Structured outputs** - Constrains the Messages API response format (`output_config.format`) and/or tool parameter validation (`strict: true`). The recommended approach is `client.messages.parse()` which validates responses against your schema automatically. Note: the old `output_format` parameter is deprecated; use `output_config: {format: {...}}` on `messages.create()`.

**Supporting endpoints** - Batches (`POST /v1/messages/batches`), Files (`POST /v1/files`), Token Counting (`POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` - see `shared/token-counting.md`), and Models (`GET /v1/models`, `GET /v1/models/{id}` - live capability/context-window discovery) feed into or support Messages API requests.

### Claude Fable 5.2 (`claude-fable-5-2`) - most capable widely released model

Claude Fable 5.2 is Anthropic's most capable widely released model, for the most demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work; everything below also applies to **Claude Mythos 5.2** (`claude-mythos-5-2`, verified organizations only - same capabilities, pricing, and API surface, so the `refusal` handling below applies there too). 1M context window (the maximum is also the default), 128K max output. Key API differences from Opus-tier - see `shared/model-migration.md` -> Migrating to Claude Fable 5.2 (and the Claude Fable 5.1 sections it builds on) for details:

- **Thinking is always on** - omit the `thinking` parameter entirely (or send `{type: "adaptive"}`). Any other explicit configuration is rejected: `{type: "disabled"}` and `{type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}` both return a 400. Control depth with `output_config.effort` (supports `low` through `xhigh` and `max`).
- **The raw chain of thought is never returned** - responses carry regular `thinking` blocks (not `redacted_thinking`): `display: "summarized"` returns a readable summary, `"omitted"` (the default) leaves the `thinking` field as an empty string. Replay rules: pass thinking blocks back unchanged on the same model; other models drop them silently (unbilled - nothing to strip; Claude Mythos 5.2 instead reads them); details in `shared/model-migration.md`.
- **Tokenizer** - same tokenizer as Opus 4.8 (introduced with Opus 4.7). Token counts are roughly unchanged when migrating from Opus 4.7/4.8; per-token pricing differs. Coming from Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5, or older, re-baseline with `count_tokens` (the Opus 4.7 tokenizer uses ~1×-1.35× as many tokens).
- **`refusal` stop reason - handle it, and opt into fallbacks by default** - safety classifiers may decline a request (HTTP 200, `stop_reason: "refusal"`, with a `stop_details` category); always check `stop_reason` before reading `content`. **When you write `claude-fable-5-2`, `claude-fable-5-1`, `claude-opus-5-5`, `claude-opus-5`, or `claude-sonnet-5-5` code, include the server-side `fallbacks` parameter by default** (for `claude-sonnet-5-5`, prefer the `"default"` form: the array form may name only `claude-sonnet-5`; on platforms without server-side `fallbacks` use the SDK middleware below, except when the request sends `between_tools`: only Claude Sonnet 5.5 accepts it and the middleware re-sends the same request body on the fallback model, so write the retry yourself and send it without `between_tools` - see `shared/model-migration.md` -> Migrating to Claude Sonnet 5.5 -> Safeguards and fallback). Simplest form: `betas: ["server-side-fallback-2026-07-01"]` + `fallbacks: "default"`, which routes by refusal category so you never maintain a model list. (With the array form you name the fallback model yourself: the same beta with `fallbacks: [{"model": "claude-opus-4-8"}]`, or `claude-sonnet-5` for `claude-sonnet-5-5`. On Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry, use the SDKs' client-side `BetaRefusalFallbackMiddleware` + `BetaFallbackState`.) Tell the user you've enabled it; drop it only if they decline. Full semantics (billing, mid-stream refusals, credit repricing) in `shared/model-migration.md` -> refusal section. **Per-language code examples in `{lang}/claude-api/README.md` § Refusal Fallbacks cover the array form only** - for the `"default"` mode, send the same request with `fallbacks: "default"` (Go: `anthropic.BetaFallbacksParamOfDefault()`; C#: `new Default()`); the header doesn't change.
- **No assistant prefill** - same as the rest of the 4.6+ family.
- **30-day data retention required** - Claude Fable 5.2 is not available under zero data retention unless expressly authorized by Anthropic; requests from an org whose retention configuration doesn't meet the requirement return `400 invalid_request_error`.
- **Longer turns, different prompting** - single requests on hard tasks can run many minutes (plan timeouts/streaming/progress UX); effort sweeps should include low/medium for routine work; prompts written for prior models are often too prescriptive and reduce output quality. See `shared/model-migration.md` -> Migrating to Claude Fable 5.2 -> Choosing an effort level and Behavioral shifts (prompt-tunable) for the recommended prompt snippets, and Migrating to Claude Fable 5.1 -> Behavioral shifts -> Longer turns by default for planning long turns.
- **Successor to Claude Fable 5.1 (`claude-fable-5-1`, still served) at a lower price - $8 / $40 per MTok, cache reads $0.20.** Same surface (forced `tool_choice` `any` / `tool` 400s, preserved thinking and, in beta, per-message `effort`, turn-scoped `clear_at` system messages and `thinking.display: "updates"`) with four breaking changes: the history-editing check is enforced for **every** account, on Claude Mythos 5.2 too (make every harness append-only and run the three-step check); no model released earlier reads its thinking blocks, Claude Fable 5.1 included, and they work only in the account that produced them or one linked to it; `computer_20251124` 400s on every platform except Amazon Bedrock (use `computer_toolset_20260801`); and with the advisor tool a Claude Fable 5.2 executor accepts only `claude-fable-5-2` or `claude-mythos-5-2` as its advisor. No structured outputs in an organization using customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK). ## Authentication (Quick Reference)

**An unset `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` does NOT mean there are no credentials.** The SDKs and the `ant` CLI resolve credentials in this order (first match wins): `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` -> `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` -> the `ANTHROPIC_PROFILE`-selected or active OAuth profile from `ant auth login` -> Workload Identity Federation env vars -> the default profile on disk. A bare `Anthropic()` / `new Anthropic()` / `anthropic.NewClient()` works after `ant auth login` with no env var set.

**When you need to call the API and `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is unset, don't ask the user for a key.** First run `ant auth status` and read its `Credentials` block, not the `Active profile:` line. If the block has an `(active)` row:

- **SDK code or `ant` CLI:** just run it. The zero-arg client constructor and every `ant ...` subcommand pick up that credential automatically (a platform row needs that platform's SDK client).
- **Raw `curl` / HTTP (`Profile` row):** get a short-lived token with `ant auth print-credentials --access-token` and send it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>` **plus** the header `anthropic-beta: oauth-2025-04-20` (OAuth tokens go on `Authorization: Bearer`, not `x-api-key:` - converting a curl from an API key is a header change, not a key swap). Always pass `--access-token`; the no-flag form prints JSON, not a bare token.

Only ask the user for a key if `ant auth status` reports no `(active)` credential (or `ant` itself isn't installed). Suggest `ant auth login` as the first option - it stores a profile under `~/.config/anthropic/` that the SDKs read automatically - and an exported `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` as the alternative.

Full auth details (named profiles, scopes, the API-key-shadows-profile trap, refresh-token expiry): `shared/anthropic-cli.md`.

Use adaptive thinking (`thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`) on every current model except Haiku 4.5, which still takes `budget_tokens` (table below) - Claude dynamically decides when and how much to think. Per-model rules:

| Model | Thinking config | Omitting `thinking` | `budget_tokens` | Sampling (`temperature`/`top_p`/`top_k`) | Effort levels |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
