content.text: Shown in the next-step box. Your closing message is your answer to the user: write it now, in full, as the last thing you say this turn. The box asks your question, so do not ask it again.

Phase 1 is done. The app now has 5,000 mock users, seeded automatically the first time the server starts, and I checked it in Docker. Nothing is committed yet.

**What a user has:**
- name, email, phone, city, language (`tr` for 85%, `en` for 15%)
- SMS and email consent
- order count and total spent
- the date they last added something to their cart, and the date of their last purchase

**How the data is made:**
- **Repeatable:** the same seed always gives exactly the same users, so test numbers and demo numbers don't drift.
- **Clearly fake:** names come from fixed Turkish and English lists, emails are on reserved `example.com/.org/.net` domains, and phones use the Turkish mobile format.
- **Mix:** about 70% have SMS consent and 80% email consent. Istanbul is the largest city at about 35%.
- **Bad contact details on purpose:** about 0.5% of phones and emails are malformed, so the mock provider will reject some sends permanently and we can test that path.
- **Turkish city spelling:** cities are stored as `İstanbul`, `İzmir`, and so on. The segment engine in the next phase has to match "Istanbul" typed without the Turkish dotted İ.

**A fix found by the tests:** at first the example brief (Istanbul users who added to their cart in the last 30 days and haven't bought) matched only 155 users. Cart dates were spread evenly over 90 days. They now cluster around recent days, as real shopping activity does, and the brief matches **322 users**. A test fails if a later change pushes that below 250.

**Seeding on start:** the server only seeds when the users table is empty, and a database lock stops two copies of the server seeding at once.

All 9 test packages pass under `-race`. DECISIONS and the README status line are updated. The pixel-grid plan update from earlier isn't committed either.

input.new_string:
## Segment rules

- **One field catalog drives everything** (`internal/segment/fields.go`): the JSON schema Claude must follow,
  validation, the SQL column for each field, and the UI's field list (`GET /api/segments/fields`). The schema
  is generated from the catalog, so they cannot drift apart.
- **No text from a rule ever reaches SQL.** Columns and operators come from the catalog, and values are always
  `$n` parameters. Text values must be one of the catalog's known values, so an injection attempt fails as
  "unknown city" before compiling.
- **At most two levels** ("A and (B or C)"). Structured outputs don't allow recursive schemas, and deeper logic
  is hard for a marketer to read anyway.
- **Consent is not a rule field.** It's applied per channel at send time, so no rule can reach users who didn't
  consent.
- **Validation lists every problem with its path** (`conditions[1].value: …`), so one round trip to Claude
  can fix them all.
- **Strings are not accepted as numbers** (`"30"` is rejected), so mistakes surface instead of being guessed at.
- **"Within N days" is anchored to one `now`,** so a preview and the send that follows can use the same cut-off.
- **Tests compare results with hand-written SQL.** They also check that opposite operators split the users
  exactly (e.g. `within_days 45` + `not_within_days 45` = everyone, which catches a forgotten `NULL`), and
  that 200 random catalog rules all run.

Phase 2 is done: audience rules now become safe SQL, and the preview endpoint returns live counts. Nothing from Phase 2 is committed yet.

**How a rule is handled** (`internal/segment`):
- **Catalog:** one list of allowed fields: city, language, order count, total spent, last purchase, last cart, signup date. From it come the JSON schema Claude will have to follow, the validation, the SQL column for each field, and the field list the UI will show. The schema is generated from the catalog, so they can't fall out of sync.
- **Validation:** every problem comes back with its location, e.g. `conditions[1].value: unknown city "Paris"; allowed: İstanbul, …`. Claude can fix them all in one retry, and the UI can show them next to the rule.
- **Normalization:** "istanbul", "ISTANBUL" and " İstanbul " all become `İstanbul`; duplicate values in a list are removed.
- **Compilation:** column names and operators come only from the catalog, and every value is passed as a `$n` query parameter. An injection attempt like `x' OR '1'='1` doesn't reach SQL at all; it's rejected as an unknown city.
- **Consent can't be targeted.** It isn't a rule field and will be applied per channel when sending.

**Endpoints:**
- `GET /api/segments/fields` returns the fields, their operators and their allowed values.
- `POST /api/segments/preview` returns the cleaned-up rule, the total match count, how many each channel can reach, and 5 sample users. A bad rule gets a 422 with the list of problems.

**Tests:**
- **Same numbers as plain SQL:** the example brief gives the same counts as a query I wrote by hand: 322 users, 231 reachable by SMS, 265 by email.
- **Opposites cover everyone:** each pair of opposite conditions (e.g. "bought in the last 45 days" and "not in the last 45 days") must add up to all 5,000 users.
- **Random rules:** 200 random rules built from the catalog all run without a SQL error.
- **Checked against a planted bug:** when I removed the "or never bought" part on purpose, both tests failed. The original is restored.
- **In Docker:** the same rule gives the same 322 users.

All 10 test packages pass under `-race`. The Docker stack is still running on http://localhost:8080 if you want to try the preview endpoint.

input.new_string:
## LLM integration

- **Official Anthropic Go SDK** behind a small `Provider` interface (ported from my earlier project). Every call
  streams.
- **JSON comes from structured outputs** (`output_config.format`), not a forced tool call. Newer models reject
  forced `tool_choice`, and structured outputs keep the answer's shape fixed.
- **The backend validates what the schema can't express:** known fields and values, number ranges, and later
  message lengths.
- **One retry policy.** The SDK's own retries are off, and ours retries 429/5xx/529 with backoff and jitter,
  honoring `Retry-After`. Errors after text has streamed are never retried, so an answer is never shown twice.
- **One repair round.** If the answer fails validation, Claude gets one fresh request with the rejected answer and
  every problem listed. A second failure is shown to the marketer, who can reword the brief or edit the rule by
  hand. The rejected answer is quoted in a new user message, not replayed as an assistant turn, which keeps
  requests valid under newer models' history checks.
- **Errors map to what the user can do:**

  | Code | Meaning |
  | --- | --- |
  | `llm_invalid_output` (422) | The answer was still invalid after the repair round. |
  | `llm_refused` (422) | The model declined the brief. |
  | `llm_unavailable` (502) | Temporary: try again. |
  | `llm_rejected` (502) | Configuration: bad key, missing workspace. |

  A real call found the last one: an organization key needs `ANTHROPIC_WORKSPACE_ID`, and the first version
  wrongly said "try again".
- **Without an API key, a keyword-based mock** answers in the same JSON shapes and goes through the same
  validation, so the app works offline. Tests use a separate scripted fake.
- **The brief sits in `<brief>` tags,** and the prompt treats it as a description of the campaign, not as
  instructions.

**What Phase 3 adds:**
- **LLM layer** (ported from agents-platform): the provider interface, retry with backoff and `Retry-After`, and the scripted fake for tests.
- **Claude adapter** on Anthropic's official Go SDK.
  - Every call streams.
  - JSON comes back through structured outputs, at low effort.
  - The SDK's own retries are off, so there's one retry policy.
  - The refusal fallback is sent only for models that support it (not Haiku).
  - Your key is scrubbed from any error text.

- **Audience step:**
  - The prompt's field list is generated from the same catalog the validator uses.
  - The brief goes inside `<brief>` tags, and the model is told to treat it as a campaign description, not instructions.
  - One repair round: a rejected answer goes back to Claude once, with every problem listed.
  - A "refine with an instruction" option sends the current rule plus the instruction.
- **Campaigns:** a table and these endpoints:
  - `POST /api/campaigns`
  - `GET /api/campaigns`
  - `GET /api/campaigns/{id}`
  - `POST /api/campaigns/{id}/audience`
  - `POST /api/campaigns/{id}/audience/refine`
  - `PUT /api/campaigns/{id}/audience` for hand edits

  Each failure gets an error code the UI can act on, and a failed generation leaves the campaign as a draft so it can be retried.
- **Keyword mock for running without a key.** It answers in the same JSON, which goes through the same checks. It handles English and Turkish briefs: the example brief gives the same rule and the same 322 users as Claude should.

3. **There's a Postgres installed directly on your Mac, also using port 5432.** So when I said earlier that the project's Postgres was on 5432, that was wrong: a database client would have opened your local Postgres. The Docker Postgres is now on port **55432**.

## Messages

- **One language per campaign**, `tr` or `en`. By default the model uses the brief's language. If the marketer
  picks one, the schema's `language` enum is narrowed to it, so the model cannot answer in another.
- **Limits are checked after personalization against this audience,** not the template alone. The backend reads
  the longest first name, last name and city among the matched users and renders the worst case. An SMS that fits
  for "Ankara" can be too long for "Eskişehir". Changing the audience re-checks existing messages: they become
  `invalid` (with the reason) or stay `ready`, without being rewritten.
- **SMS encoding is reported, not enforced.** The requirement is ≤ 160 characters. Turkish letters (ş, ğ, ı, İ)
  switch an SMS to UCS-2, where one part holds 70 characters, so a 149-character Turkish SMS goes out as 3 parts.
  The check shows encoding and part count so the marketer can decide.
- **Generation is a queue job, not part of the HTTP request.** The request answers 202 at once. Text streams to
  the campaign's SSE stream as field deltas (`{"attempt","field","text"}`), extracted from Claude's partial JSON
  by a streaming parser. A page refresh or server restart doesn't lose the result, and temporary LLM errors are
  retried by the queue.
- **Newest wins.** Every generation request or hand edit bumps `content_version`, and a job saves only if the
  version is still its own. While a generation runs, the audience is locked (409 `generating`).
- **Hand edits pass the same checks** as generated messages (`PUT /content`, 422 with every problem).
- **The database must be UTF-8.** Embedded Postgres defaulted to `SQL_ASCII`, where `char_length('Eskişehir')`
  is 10 (bytes), not 9. A test caught this through a wrong SMS length. Embedded databases are now created as
  UTF-8, the server refuses to start on any other encoding, and a test fails if a test database isn't UTF-8.

**How it works:**
- **Background job:** "Generate messages" answers at once and the work runs as a queue job, so refreshing the page or restarting the server doesn't lose it.
- **Live boxes:** a streaming JSON parser pulls each field out of Claude's partial answer, so the SMS, subject and email body fill in live.

- **Audience changes re-check messages:** they're marked invalid with the reason, and become valid again if you change the audience back.
- **Hand edits:** they go through the same checks.
- **Newest wins:** a newer generation or a hand edit always beats an older generation still running. While one is running, the audience is locked.

1. **Test databases weren't UTF-8.** They came out as `SQL_ASCII`, where Postgres counts bytes, so "Eskişehir" measured 10 characters. A test caught it through a wrong SMS length. -- at the database level: approving twice, or a retried approval, inserts nothing new.

    user_id             bigint      NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id),
    channel             text        NOT NULL CHECK (channel IN ('sms', 'email')),
    status              text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'queued'
                        CHECK (status IN ('queued', 'sending', 'retrying', 'sent',
                                          'delivered', 'undelivered', 'failed')),
    attempts            int         NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    provider_message_id text        UNIQUE,
    last_error          text        NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    created_at          timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at          timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    sent_at             timestamptz,
    receipt_at          timestamptz,
    UNIQUE (campaign_id, user_id, channel)
);

input.new_string:
## Sending

- **Approval is one transaction.** It re-checks the messages against the audience as it is now ("within 30 days"
  shifts with time). It inserts every delivery with `INSERT … SELECT` (consent filter per channel) and every send
  job the same way, then moves the campaign to `sending`. It all commits together or not at all. A second approve
  answers 409 and inserts nothing.
- **Never twice: four independent layers.**
  1. `UNIQUE (campaign_id, user_id, channel)` on deliveries.
  2. One job per delivery under a unique dedup key.
  3. A worker skips a delivery that is already finished.
  4. An `Idempotency-Key` per delivery sent to the provider, which answers a repeat with its first result. Only
     this covers "the provider accepted the message but its response was lost".

  The chaos test proves it. A mutation that sends a fresh key per attempt makes it fail with deliveries accepted
  twice.
- **Retries.**
  - 429, 5xx and network errors are retried with exponential backoff and jitter (1 s base, 60 s cap), or after
    the provider's `Retry-After`, up to 6 attempts.
  - Other 4xx (invalid number or email) fail at once.
  - When the queue gives up, the delivery is marked `failed`.
- **Rate limit:** a token bucket per channel (`golang.org/x/time/rate`), 100/s with a burst of 1, so the limit
  also holds over short windows. Each channel has its own worker pool (40 workers, enough for ~100/s at the mock's
  50–500 ms latency), and every send waits for its channel's limiter. The limiter is per process: with several app
  replicas it would need to move to Postgres or Redis. A test checks that no one-second window exceeds the limit.
- **Receipts by signed webhook.**
  - The signature is HMAC-SHA256 over `timestamp.body`; requests older than 5 minutes are refused.
  - Receipts are matched by our delivery ID (the provider echoes it as `reference`), because a receipt can arrive
    before the worker has saved the provider's message ID.
  - Status only moves forward. Duplicate and late receipts change nothing.
  - A `delivered` receipt also overrides our own `failed`: we gave up, but the provider had accepted the message.
  - Unknown or duplicate receipts get 200, so the provider stops retrying; database errors get 500, so it retries.
- **Campaign completion:** `completed` once no delivery is queued, sending or retrying. Receipts may still arrive
  afterwards and update deliveries.
- **Live doorbells are throttled** to one per campaign every 250 ms, with a trailing ring, so thousands of status
  changes cost a few notifications a second.
- **Metrics on `/metrics`:**
  - provider calls by status code, with latency;
  - finished deliveries;
  - webhooks by outcome;
  - LLM calls and tokens by task;
  - queue depth, read from the jobs table at scrape time.

  The Docker run caught permanent failures being counted twice: both the handler and the queue's `OnFailed`
  "succeeded" in marking the same row. Now the second update skips rows already failed, and the chaos test compares
  the counter with the database.
- **Mock provider:** a separate service (`cmd/mockprovider`), with every misbehaviour set by an environment
  variable. In Docker, a 2,623-message campaign finished in about 24 s with 0 duplicates, and the 14 failures were
  exactly the malformed contacts.

Phase 5, sending, is done. A real 2,623-message campaign in Docker finished in about 24 seconds, and nobody received a message twice. All 15 test packages pass; Phase 5 isn't committed yet.

**What was built:**
- **Mock provider:** a separate service, `cmd/mockprovider`, that misbehaves on purpose. It answers with random 500s, 429s with `Retry-After`, its own rate limit, slow responses, lost responses and 400s for bad contacts, and it sends signed receipts that come twice, late, or early. Every behaviour is set by an environment variable, and `GET /stats` on port 9090 shows what it saw.
- **Approval:** one transaction re-checks the messages, inserts all deliveries and their send jobs with the consent filter, and starts sending. A second approve returns 409 and changes nothing.
- **Sending:**
  - One worker pool per channel, each capped at 100/s by a token bucket with a burst of 1.
  - 429, 5xx and network errors are retried with backoff, or after `Retry-After`.
  - Bad contacts fail on the first attempt.
- **Receipts:** a webhook verifies the HMAC signature and timestamp. Status only moves forward, so duplicates and late receipts change nothing. A receipt that beats the send response still lands, because it's matched by our delivery ID.
- **Metrics on `/metrics`:** provider calls by status code with latency, finished deliveries, webhooks, LLM calls and tokens, and queue depth.

**What proves it:**
- **Chaos test:** a whole campaign against the misbehaving provider, run in every `make test`. Every delivered message was accepted exactly once, the only failures were the malformed contacts, and the chaos really happened (server errors, 429s, lost responses, replays).
- **Planted bug:** sending a fresh idempotency key on each attempt makes the test fail with deliveries accepted twice.
- **Rate-limit test:** no one-second window goes over the limit.
- **Docker run:**

| Measure | Result |
|---|---|
| Messages queued | 2,623 (1,220 SMS, 1,403 email) |
| Accepted by the provider | 2,609, exactly delivered + undelivered |
| Duplicate acceptances | 0 |
| Failed | 14, exactly the malformed contacts, each rejected with a 400 on the first try |
| Survived along the way | 178 rate-limit responses, 139 server errors, 20 lost responses |

**Problems found and fixed along the way:**
1. **A test that couldn't see one safety layer.** In the first chaos test, 42 lost responses produced 0 replays. 3. **Receipts rejected as stale in tests.** The webhook was checking timestamps against the clock that tests pin to a fixed date, so real receipts looked days old. It now always uses real time.

input.new_string:
## Live delivery progress

- **Progress is computed, not stored per change.** Workers only ring a throttled doorbell (≤ 4/s per campaign).
  The stream then sends a `progress` snapshot at most every 500 ms, with a trailing send so the final state always
  arrives. 10,000 status changes therefore cost about two small queries a second per viewer, not 10,000 events.
- **One query builds the snapshot:**
  - counts per channel and status;
  - throughput over the last 5 s;
  - retries;
  - receipts still pending;
  - a **grid string**: one character per delivery in delivery order (`q s r t d u f`). The dashboard's pixel
    grid draws one square per character. About 2,600 deliveries make a ~2.6 KB string, small enough to resend
    whole each time instead of diffing.
- **Stored events and snapshots share one SSE stream.** A reconnecting browser replays missed stored events from
  `Last-Event-ID` and gets a fresh snapshot at once.
- **The stream ends only when nothing more will change:** sending finished and every receipt in, with a 2-minute
  grace period for receipts that never come. The "is it finished" check reads the cheap campaign status first and
  builds the full snapshot only after sending is done.
- **In Docker,** a 2,623-message campaign streamed 46 snapshots over 24 s, about 90 msg/s per channel at the
  100/s limit, and the stream closed itself once the last receipt arrived.

Phase 5 is committed as `be175d6`, and Phase 6 is done: the campaign event stream now shows delivery progress live. Phase 6 isn't committed yet. All test packages pass.

**What the stream now sends.** After approval, `GET /api/campaigns/{id}/events` sends a `progress` event at most every 500 ms. A final one always goes out, so the last state is never missed. Each event carries:
- counts per channel and status;
- throughput over the last 5 seconds;
- the number of retries;
- how many receipts are still pending;
- **the pixel-grid data:** one character per delivery, in order (`q` queued, `s` sending, `r` retrying, `t` sent, `d` delivered, `u` undelivered, `f` failed). The dashboard will draw one square per character.

**Why it stays cheap:** workers only ring a doorbell at most 4 times a second per campaign. The stream turns that into about two small queries a second per viewer, instead of one event per status change.

**When the stream ends:** only once nothing more will change. Sending must be finished and every receipt in, with a 2-minute grace period for receipts that never come. A reconnecting browser replays the stored events it missed and gets a fresh snapshot straight away.

**Docker run, 2,623 messages:**
- 46 progress events over 23.6 seconds.
- About 90 messages a second per channel, under the 100/s limit.
- The retry count climbs as retries happen, and pending receipts fall to 0 after sending ends.
- The stream closed itself after the last receipt.
- A slice of the SMS grid mid-send: `udddudddddddrdddddddddddddddrdddddd…`

**New test:** it checks that progress events are throttled, that the final snapshot has fully settled (only delivered, undelivered or failed), that the grid agrees with the counts, and that the number of squares matches the deliveries in the database.

cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
# Frontend: Vue + Vite build.
FROM node:22-alpine AS web
WORKDIR /web
COPY web/package.json web/package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY web/ ./
RUN npm run build

# Backend: the server and the mock provider.
FROM golang:1.27-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/server ./cmd/server && \
    CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o /out/mockprovider ./cmd/mockprovider

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=build /out/server /out/mockprovider /
COPY --from=web /web/dist /web
ENV WEB_DIR=/web
EXPOSE 8080 9090
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]
EOF

.git

bin
web/node_modules
web/dist
ai-sessions
*.local
CLAUDE.local.md

cat > Makefile <<'EOF'
.PHONY: up down run web test test-go test-web vet build session

up:
	docker compose up --build

down:
	docker compose down -v

# Run the API locally (embedded Postgres when DATABASE_URL is unset). Serves
# web/dist if it has been built; use `make web` for the dev server with reload.
run:
	go run ./cmd/server

web:
	cd web && npm install && npm run dev

build:
	go build -o bin/server ./cmd/server
	cd web && npm ci && npm run build

# All tests. No API key, Docker or network needed (Postgres is embedded).
test: test-go test-web

test-go:
	go test -race ./...

test-web:
	cd web && (test -d node_modules || npm ci) && npm test

vet:
	go vet ./...
	cd web && npx vue-tsc --noEmit

# Scrub a Claude app session export into ai-sessions/.
# Usage: make session IN=~/Downloads/session-export-123.zip NAME=01-scaffold
session:
	@test -n "$(IN)" || (echo "usage: make session IN=<export.zip> NAME=<name>" && exit 2)
	go run ./tools/sessionexport -in "$(IN)" -name "$(NAME)"
EOF

input.new_string:
## Frontend

- **Stack:**
  - Vue 3 (`<script setup>`, TypeScript), vue-router, Vite and Tailwind v4.
  - Design tokens from my earlier project (shadcn neutral with a warm tint, Geist font, 0.625rem radius).
  - Small hand-written components instead of the shadcn-vue CLI, to keep dependencies few.
  - Fonts are self-hosted through `@fontsource`.
- **One origin.** The Go server serves the built app (`WEB_DIR`, with an `index.html` fallback for client
  routes), so no CORS is needed. In development, Vite proxies `/api` to the server.
- **Live updates through `EventSource`,** which reconnects by itself with `Last-Event-ID`. Message text streams
  into the editors and previews as `delta` events. A new attempt number (the repair round) clears the boxes and
  starts over.
- **The pixel grid is a `<canvas>`,** one square per delivery coloured by status, drawn from the `progress`
  event's grid string. Thousands of squares redrawn twice a second would be slow as DOM elements. Hovering a square
  shows its status. The status colours come from CSS variables shared with the badges and bars.
- **The SMS counter mirrors the server's check in TypeScript** (worst-case length against the audience's longest
  names, GSM-7 vs UCS-2 parts), so it updates as the marketer types. The server still validates on save and at
  approval. The audience's longest values are saved with the audience (`audience_longest`), so both sides measure
  the same thing.
- **Rule chips:** edit a value in place, remove a condition, or "refine" with an instruction to Claude. Every edit
  goes through the same server validation, and errors come back with the full list of problems.
- **Approval has a confirm step** that shows the exact number of messages.
- **Checked in the browser:** a Turkish brief went through audience (auto-started), streamed messages, approval
  and the live dashboard, at desktop and phone width, with no console errors. That walk-through caught auto-start
  silently doing nothing: the step's component wasn't rendered yet when it was called. It's fixed with `nextTick`.

content.text: Shown in the next-step box. Your closing message is your answer to the user: write it now, in full, as the last thing you say this turn. The box asks your question, so do not ask it again.

Campaigns now run on their own from the brief to "Ready to send", and the home page has the new hero. All tests pass, and Docker serves everything on http://localhost:8080. Nothing from Phase 7 or these changes is committed yet.

**Why you still had to click "Write messages":** your browser tab was most likely still running the old version of the app. A web app like this keeps its loaded code until the page is fully reloaded, and the old screens had that button. The server was already serving the new screens, which don't have it.

Even so, you found a real weakness: the step from audience to messages lived only in the browser, so an old tab, or closing it at the wrong moment, left campaigns half done. I've moved that step to the server. As soon as the AI finishes the audience, the server queues the messages itself. I checked it with a fresh campaign: the audience request came back with messages already being written, and 4 seconds later it was ready to send, with welcome copy matching the audience. Please do a full reload (Cmd+Shift+R) on any old tab.

**The hero, in our own wording, colours and graphics:**
- **Left:** a huge two-line uppercase headline, "BRIEF IN. / DELIVERED."
- **Right**, behind a thin vertical rule: a justified uppercase tagline, the pixel logo, one short line of text and a "Start a campaign" button.
- **Below:** a full-width band of small squares in blue, navy and yellow with a few red. It's solid at the top, breaks into drips at the bottom, and drifts slowly. It stops moving if your system is set to reduce motion, or when the tab is hidden.

content.text:
All three make sense; I'll add them. The resend button needs a little backend design to keep the "never twice" guarantee.

**How resend will work:**
- **What gets resent:** deliveries the provider reported as undelivered, and those that failed after running out of retries.
- **What doesn't:** messages that failed permanently, such as a malformed phone number or email. Sending those again would just fail again, so they're marked as such and skipped.
- **Each resend is a new round.** Every round gets its own idempotency key and provider reference (`123.1` for round 1). So within a round, each message still goes out exactly once. A late receipt from the old round can't mark the new send as delivered.
- **When it's available:** only after the campaign has finished sending. The campaign then goes back to `sending`, and the live dashboard reconnects and follows the resend.

content.text: Shown in the next-step box. Your closing message is your answer to the user: write it now, in full, as the last thing you say this turn. The box asks your question, so do not ask it again.

Everything from this round is in, and the 1M-delivery benchmark found three real scale problems; I haven't built those fixes yet. All tests pass and Docker serves the latest version on http://localhost:8080. Nothing is committed yet.

**Done this round:**
- **Flowing band:** it scrolls continuously. New squares enter at the right as queued (grey), turn sending (yellow), then sent (blue), and settle on their real final status, delivered (navy) or not delivered (red). The final colours come from your latest 2,000 real messages, the dripping bottom edge moves with the band, and the legend lists all five stages.
- **Hero:** plain white with no grid behind it, and one "Start a campaign" button. The header's button is hidden on the home page only.
- **"Yes, send" double-click:** I couldn't make it fail in four tries, but I found a window where the button looked idle again right after a successful send. It now stays busy until the dashboard appears, and the page switches using the approved campaign straight away. If sending fails, the reason shows next to the button. Resend got the same treatment.
- **Smaller requests:** an "All campaigns" link on campaign pages, a pointer cursor on buttons, and a Resend button for messages that didn't arrive (invalid contacts are skipped). It covered the stale-receipt and exactly-once cases, and one click worked in the browser.

**Scaling to a million users**

The case's own limit sets the pace: 100 messages per second per channel. A campaign to 500,000 people is about 83 minutes of sending per channel. That's fine, but every screen and query has to stay cheap for that long. I measured with 1,000,000 deliveries on a throwaway database:

1. **Live dashboard (the one you suspected).** The snapshot takes **3.8 seconds** and carries a **1 MB** square-per-message string, and it runs every 500 ms for every viewer. Even counts alone take 115 ms.
   - **Fix:** a fixed-size grid of about 2,000 squares, each standing for a bucket of messages and coloured by its worst status, so the UI costs the same at any size.
   - **Fix:** counts kept in a small counters table, computed once per campaign per second and shared by all viewers.
2. **Approval.** Inserting 1M deliveries plus 1M jobs in one transaction takes **15.6 seconds**, so the "Yes, send" request would hang or time out.
   - **Fix:** approval answers immediately and fans out in background batches of about 10,000 rows. The unique key already makes each batch safe to repeat.
3. **Two rows and constant updates per message.** That's 296 MB plus 268 MB per million messages, and nothing is ever deleted.
   - **Fix:** use the deliveries row itself as the queue, which halves the writes, and delete finished jobs after a few days.

**Smaller points worth noting in the docs:**
- **Rate limiter:** it lives in one process. With several app replicas, the 100/s limit would multiply, so it would need to move to Postgres or Redis.
- **Provider outage:** a breaker per channel should pause sending, instead of a million jobs cycling through retries.
- **Audience preview:** counting 1M users takes about 100–300 ms without indexes; acceptable, and indexes on the filter columns help.
- **The "Not delivered" list:** needs an index to stay fast when sorted.
- **Already fine at this size:**
  - The queue's claim stays at 10 ms with 400,000 jobs waiting.
  - Live updates are throttled.
  - The LLM runs once per campaign, not once per person.
  - The exactly-once guarantees don't depend on size.
- **Home band:** I removed its unnecessary row count, so it now reads only the newest rows and costs the same at any size.

content.text:
**What "CI" means**

CI (continuous integration) is a small config file in the repo, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. Every time code is pushed to GitHub, GitHub's own servers check out the code and run the same checks we run with `make test`: all Go tests, the frontend tests, the type check, and a build. Then they put a green ✓ or a red ✗ next to the commit.

Why it's worth having:
- **It's on the case's bonus list.**
- **Reviewers see that the tests really pass on a clean machine**, not just on yours. Our tests need no API key and no Docker (Postgres is embedded), so they run there as they are.
- **It's cheap:** one file, roughly 30 lines.

It only does anything once the repo is on GitHub, which the deliverables require anyway.

**100 languages for 10,000 users**

Yes, I'd translate with Claude, but **once per language, not once per user.** The messages are templates with `{{first_name}}` in them, so one translated template serves everyone who speaks that language:

- **Calls:** at most one per language in the audience. For 100 languages that's 100 calls of about 1,500 tokens each, roughly **$0.03 on Haiku**. The number of users makes no difference.
- **How:** write the main version in the brief's language, then have Claude *adapt* it to each language rather than translate word by word. It keeps the tone and the offer, uses the same JSON format, and runs through the same checks:
  - the variables must stay exactly the same (`{{first_name}}` must not become `{{ad}}`);
  - SMS ≤ 160 characters and subject ≤ 80, with the length worked out per language. Scripts like Arabic, Russian or Chinese always need UCS-2, so 70 characters per SMS part;
  - a language that fails gets the same one repair round as today.
- **Running 100 calls:** one queue job per language, with limited concurrency so we stay under Anthropic's rate limits. The queue we already have does exactly this. Retries, live progress ("62 of 100 languages ready") and "newest version wins" come for free.
- **Sending:** each user gets the version in their stored language. Anyone whose language is missing or failed falls back to the main language.
- **Review:** nobody can read 100 languages, so the review page would show the main version plus one status per language (ready, too long, failed). It would also list sample previews to spot-check, still with one "Send" at the end.
- **Brand safety:** a glossary for terms that must never be translated (brand and product names), and caching by text so unchanged copy isn't translated again. A human check matters only for markets where the wording is regulated.

In our mock data users only speak `tr` and `en`, so the bonus would cover those two, but the same design works unchanged for 100. If you want this bonus, the 2–3 hours I estimated earlier still holds, because the per-language job design is the same at 2 languages or 100.

Shall I commit what's done and then add CI and scheduled sending?

All three bonus features are built and tested, and the Docker stack on http://localhost:8080 runs them. Phase 7 is committed as `3c30b45`; these three features aren't committed yet.

**1. CI** (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`). On every push, GitHub runs three checks:
- the Go tests, with `go vet` and a formatting check;
- the frontend type check, tests and build;
- a Docker image build.

It needs no secrets, because tests use the mock LLM and an embedded Postgres. The file is valid, but it hasn't actually run, since the repo isn't on GitHub yet; it runs on the first push.

**2. Scheduled sending.** "Schedule" on the review page opens a date and time picker.
- **Audience:** fixed when you schedule, so it's the people you reviewed.
- **Cancel:** the dashboard shows "Scheduled for … (in N min)" with "Cancel schedule", which takes the campaign back to Ready to send.
- **Limits:** the time must be 1 minute to 30 days ahead.
- **Two bugs found on the way:**
  - A test caught the check accepting a time in the past, because it used the pinned test clock. It now uses real time.
  - In the browser, the default time was rounded *down* (an hour from 2:47 PM became 3:00 PM). It now rounds up, so it's always at least an hour ahead.

**3. Each user in their own language.**
- **Translation:** once the main messages are ready, the server checks which languages the reachable audience speaks and queues one translation per extra language. That's never one per user, so 100 languages means at most 100 short calls.
- **Checks:** a translation must keep exactly the same `{{variables}}`, and passes the length checks measured for that language's own users.
- **Sending:** each person gets their language's version. Anyone whose translation failed, is outdated or is missing gets the main language.
- **Review page:** language tabs, e.g. "Türkçe · main | English · 45". Edits to the main version re-translate automatically, and Send waits while translations are being written.
- **Real result:** for your Turkish İstanbul cart brief, Haiku's English version reads naturally: "Oğuz, the items in your cart are waiting for you! Complete your order now with 20% off."

**Tests:** in a real send, each user receives the SMS in their own language. A failed or outdated translation falls back to Turkish, a translation that drops `{{city}}` goes to the repair round, and scheduling (waiting, validation, cancel) is covered. Everything passes, including `make test`.

**A/B variants** are left out on purpose. Both the README and DECISIONS.md explain why: without opens or clicks, there's nothing meaningful to compare.

What's left is Phase 8: the architecture write-up in the README, and exporting this session into `ai-sessions/` with the scrubber.

content.content:
# Smart Campaign Composer

A marketer describes a campaign in plain language. Claude turns it into a validated audience segment and
SMS/email copy. The marketer reviews and approves, and the system sends through a rate-limited queue to a mock
provider while a dashboard shows delivery status live.

> Status: the core flow is complete: brief → AI audience → AI messages → approval → sending → live dashboard.
> Remaining: architecture write-up and session exports (phase 8), then bonus features.
> See [docs/PLAN.md](docs/PLAN.md) for the phases.

## Quick start

```bash
cp .env.example .env   # optional: add ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, otherwise the mock LLM is used
docker compose up
```

Open http://localhost:8080.

| Command      | What it does                                  |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| `make up`    | Build and start everything with Docker Compose |
| `make run`   | Run the API locally (serves `web/dist` if built) |
| `make web`   | Frontend dev server with hot reload on :5173 (proxies the API on :8080) |
| `make test`  | Run all Go and frontend tests (no API key, Docker or network needed) |
| `make session IN=<zip> NAME=<name>` | Scrub a Claude session export into `ai-sessions/` ([how](ai-sessions/README.md)) |

### Services

| Service | Port | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `server` | 8080 | Web app, API, workers, `/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/metrics` |
| `mockprovider` | 9090 | Fake SMS/email provider; `GET /stats` shows what it saw |
| `postgres` | 55432 | `composer` / `composer` (local only) |

### API

| Endpoint | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /api/campaigns` | Create a campaign from a brief |
| `GET /api/campaigns`, `GET /api/campaigns/{id}` | List / read campaigns |
| `POST /api/campaigns/{id}/audience` | Generate the audience rule with the LLM |
| `POST /api/campaigns/{id}/audience/refine` | Change the rule with an instruction |
| `PUT /api/campaigns/{id}/audience` | Save a hand-edited rule |
| `POST /api/campaigns/{id}/content` | Generate messages (streams to `/events`) |
| `PUT /api/campaigns/{id}/content` | Save hand-edited messages |
| `POST /api/campaigns/{id}/approve` | Queue one delivery per consenting recipient and channel; `{"send_at": …}` schedules it |
| `POST /api/campaigns/{id}/unschedule` | Cancel a scheduled campaign before it starts |
| `POST /api/campaigns/{id}/resend` | Send again what did not arrive (a new round; invalid contacts skipped) |
| `GET /api/campaigns/{id}/events` | Server-sent events: status changes, message text as it is written, delivery progress (counts, throughput, pixel-grid data) |
| `GET /api/campaigns/{id}/deliveries[/counts]` | Delivery list (filter by `status`) and counts |
| `GET /api/segments/fields`, `POST /api/segments/preview` | Rule fields; preview counts for a rule |
| `GET /api/deliveries/recent` | Status codes of the latest deliveries (the home page band) |
| `POST /webhooks/provider` | Signed delivery receipts from the provider |

## Architecture

To be written in full at the end. See [DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md) for the stack and the reasons behind it.

## Bonus features

Done: CI (GitHub Actions), scheduled sending, and each user in their own language (one AI translation per
language, not per user). A/B variants were left out on purpose: without opens or clicks there is nothing to
compare. Details in [DECISIONS.md › Bonus features](DECISIONS.md#bonus-features).

## Not done yet

- Architecture write-up and session exports (phase 8)
- High scale: built for thousands of users. What would break first at a million, with measurements and the fix
  for each, is in [DECISIONS.md › Known limits at high scale](DECISIONS.md#known-limits-at-high-scale).

README.md
# AI sessions

Exports of the Claude Code sessions used to build this project, with API keys and personal data removed.
Each session has two files:

- `NN-name.md`: readable conversation. Tool calls and results are collapsed and truncated.
- `NN-name.jsonl`: the full conversation record (user and assistant turns, tool calls, tool results).

## How they are produced

1. Export the session from the Claude app (session menu → Export). This gives a zip.
2. Run the scrubber:

   ```bash
   make session IN=~/Downloads/session-export-<id>.zip NAME=01-setup-and-scaffold
   ```

The scrubber (`tools/sessionexport`) keeps only the main conversation. It drops subagent transcripts,
app metadata and internal request payloads. Then it:

- replaces the home directory with `~` and the OS username with `<user>`,
- replaces email addresses with `<email>` (commit-trailer and example domains are kept),
- removes the app's list of recently used local folders,
- applies extra `find => replace` rules from a gitignored `.scrub.local` file,
- refuses to write anything if a credential-shaped string or any private term is still present.

## Sending

- **Approval is one transaction.** It re-checks the messages against the audience as it is now ("within 30 days"
  shifts with time). It inserts every delivery with `INSERT … SELECT` (consent filter per channel) and every send
  job the same way, then moves the campaign to `sending`. It all commits together or not at all. A second approve
  answers 409 and inserts nothing.
- **Never twice: four independent layers.**
  1. `UNIQUE (campaign_id, user_id, channel)` on deliveries.
  2. One job per delivery under a unique dedup key.
  3. A worker skips a delivery that is already finished.
  4. An `Idempotency-Key` per delivery sent to the provider, which answers a repeat with its first result. Only
     this covers "the provider accepted the message but its response was lost".

  The chaos test proves it. A mutation that sends a fresh key per attempt makes it fail with deliveries accepted
  twice.
- **Retries.**
  - 429, 5xx and network errors are retried with exponential backoff and jitter (1 s base, 60 s cap), or after
    the provider's `Retry-After`, up to 6 attempts.
  - Other 4xx (invalid number or email) fail at once.
  - When the queue gives up, the delivery is marked `failed`.
- **Rate limit:** a token bucket per channel (`golang.org/x/time/rate`), 100/s with a burst of 1, so the limit
  also holds over short windows. Each channel has its own worker pool (40 workers, enough for ~100/s at the mock's
  50–500 ms latency), and every send waits for its channel's limiter. The limiter is per process: with several app
  replicas it would need to move to Postgres or Redis. A test checks that no one-second window exceeds the limit.
- **Receipts by signed webhook.**
  - The signature is HMAC-SHA256 over `timestamp.body`; requests older than 5 minutes are refused.
  - Receipts are matched by our delivery ID (the provider echoes it as `reference`), because a receipt can arrive
    before the worker has saved the provider's message ID.
  - Status only moves forward. Duplicate and late receipts change nothing.
  - A `delivered` receipt also overrides our own `failed`: we gave up, but the provider had accepted the message.
  - Unknown or duplicate receipts get 200, so the provider stops retrying; database errors get 500, so it retries.
- **Campaign completion:** `completed` once no delivery is queued, sending or retrying. Receipts may still arrive
  afterwards and update deliveries.
- **Live doorbells are throttled** to one per campaign every 250 ms, with a trailing ring, so thousands of status
  changes cost a few notifications a second.
- **Metrics on `/metrics`:**
  - provider calls by status code, with latency;
  - finished deliveries;
  - webhooks by outcome;
  - LLM calls and tokens by task;
  - queue depth, read from the jobs table at scrape time.

  The Docker run caught permanent failures being counted twice: both the handler and the queue's `OnFailed`
  "succeeded" in marking the same row. Now the second update skips rows already failed, and the chaos test compares
  the counter with the database.
- **Mock provider:** a separate service (`cmd/mockprovider`), with every misbehaviour set by an environment
  variable. In Docker, a 2,623-message campaign finished in about 24 s with 0 duplicates, and the 14 failures were
  exactly the malformed contacts.

# Smart Campaign Composer A marketer describes a campaign in plain language. Claude turns it into a validated audience segment and SMS/email copy. The marketer reviews and approves once. The system then sends through a rate-limited queue to a mock provider, and a dashboard shows delivery status live. Go backend, Postgres, Vue 3 frontend. The reasons behind each choice are in [DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md). The original phased plan is in [docs/PLAN.md](docs/PLAN.md). ## Quick start ```bash docker compose up ``` Open http://localhost:8080. This runs the web app, API, workers, Postgres and the mock provider. Without an API key the server uses a **mock LLM**, so the whole flow works offline. To use Claude, create `.env` before starting: ```bash cp .env.example .env # then set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (and ANTHROPIC_WORKSPACE_ID if your key is workspace-scoped) ``` | Command | What it does | | ------------ | --------------------------------------------- | | `make up` | Build and start everything with Docker Compose | | `make test` | All Go and frontend tests. No API key, Docker or network needed | | `make run` | Run the API locally with embedded Postgres (serves `web/dist` if built) | | `make web` | Frontend dev server with hot reload on :5173 (proxies the API on :8080) | | `make session IN= NAME=` | Scrub a Claude session export into `ai-sessions/` ([how](ai-sessions/README.md)) | `make run` and `make test` need Go 1.27 and Node 22. Without `DATABASE_URL` the server starts an embedded Postgres under `.data/`. ### Services | Service | Port | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | `server` | 8080 | Web app, API, workers, `/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/metrics` | | `mockprovider` | 9090 | Fake SMS/email provider; `GET /stats` shows what it saw | | `postgres` | 55432 | `composer` / `composer` (local only) | ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR UI["Vue app
steps · review · live dashboard"] subgraph server["Go server (one binary)"] API["HTTP API + SSE"] COMP["Composer
LLM layer · validation · repair"] SEG["Segment engine
JSON rule → parameterized SQL"] W["Queue workers
content · translate · send_sms · send_email"] HUB["Event hub
LISTEN/NOTIFY"] end PG[("Postgres
users · campaigns · deliveries
jobs · events")] LLM["Claude API
(or mock LLM)"] MP["Mock provider
latency · 429 · 5xx · bad contacts"] UI -- "REST" --> API API -- "SSE: events, text deltas, progress" --> UI API --> COMP --> LLM COMP --> SEG --> PG API --> PG W -- "claim: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED" --> PG W -- "100/s per channel + Idempotency-Key" --> MP MP -- "signed webhook receipts" --> API PG -- "NOTIFY doorbell" --> HUB --> API ``` One campaign, end to end: 1. **Brief.** `POST /api/campaigns` stores the brief. 2. **Audience.** Claude returns a segment rule as JSON, using structured outputs with a schema built from the field catalog. The server validates it, and on problems sends them back for up to 2 repair rounds. It then compiles the rule to parameterized SQL and previews the audience size and samples. 3. **Messages.** A queue job asks Claude for SMS, email subject and email body, informed by audience facts (size, cities, spend, recency). The text streams to the browser field by field as it is written. It is validated against length limits and allowed variables, with the same repair loop. If users in the audience speak other languages, one translation per language is queued. 4. **Review and approve.** The marketer sees the rule as chips, the audience count, previews rendered for real recipients, and SMS length and parts. They can edit anything, and then approve once, now or at a scheduled time. 5. **Send.** Approval inserts every delivery and every send job in one transaction. Workers send at up to 100 messages/s per channel, retry temporary errors, and fail invalid contacts at once. 6. **Track.** The provider posts signed receipts (`delivered` / `undelivered`). The dashboard shows counts, throughput, retries and a pixel grid of every delivery, updated live over SSE. Failed or undelivered messages can be sent again as a new round. ## Requirements and where they are met | Requirement | How | | --- | --- | | LLM output never becomes raw SQL | The LLM returns a JSON rule (`internal/segment`). Fields, operators and value types come from one catalog. The compiler emits only parameterized SQL with whitelisted columns. Invalid rules are rejected with path-labelled problems. | | Structured LLM output, validated | Structured outputs via `output_config.format`, JSON Schema generated from Go types (`internal/schema`). Everything is still validated server-side, with a repair round that lists the problems. | | Message limits and variables | SMS 160 characters, subject 80 characters, checked at the **worst case**: the longest first name, last name and city in this audience. Only `{{first_name}}`, `{{last_name}}`, `{{city}}` are allowed. GSM-7 vs UCS-2 parts are shown (`internal/message`). | | Async queue | Postgres jobs table (`internal/queue`): `SKIP LOCKED` claims, leases, a sweeper for crashed workers, dedup keys, `run_at` for delays and schedules. | | 100 msg/s per channel | A token bucket per channel (burst 1), with its own worker pool per channel. A test checks that no one-second window goes over. | | Never the same message twice | Four layers: `UNIQUE(campaign_id, user_id, channel)`, one job per delivery under a dedup key, workers skip finished deliveries, and an `Idempotency-Key` the provider honours. A chaos test with lost responses, 429s and 5xx checks exactly-once. | | Retries | 429, 5xx and network errors back off exponentially with jitter, or honour `Retry-After`, for up to 6 attempts. Invalid contacts fail permanently, at once. | | Live status | SSE per campaign: stored events with `Last-Event-ID` replay, message deltas, and progress snapshots at most every 500 ms, woken by a throttled Postgres `NOTIFY`. | | Metrics and health | `/healthz` (process up), `/readyz` (database reachable), and Prometheus `/metrics`: provider calls and latency, deliveries, webhooks, LLM calls and tokens by task, queue depth. | | Tests with a mock LLM | `internal/llm/llmtest` scripts replies, errors and streams. The API tests run the whole flow against real Postgres (one database per test), the mock provider and the fake LLM. | ## Configuration All optional. Docker Compose sets the database, provider and webhook values for you. | Variable | Default | | | --- | --- | --- | | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | (empty → mock LLM) | | | `ANTHROPIC_WORKSPACE_ID` | (empty) | Needed for workspace-scoped keys | | `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` | `claude-haiku-5-5` | See [DECISIONS › Models](DECISIONS.md#models) | | `DATABASE_URL` | (empty → embedded Postgres in `DATA_DIR`) | Must be a UTF8 database | | `DATA_DIR` | `.data` | | | `PORT` | `8080` | | | `PROVIDER_URL` | `http://localhost:9090` | Mock provider | | `WEBHOOK_SECRET` | a dev-only value | Shared with the provider for receipt signatures | | `SEND_RATE_PER_SECOND` | `100` | Per channel | | `SEND_WORKERS` | `40` | Per channel | | `SEED_USERS` | `5000` | Mock users created on first start (deterministic) | | `WEB_DIR` | `web/dist` | Built frontend to serve | | `LOG_FORMAT` | `text` | `json` in Docker | The mock provider's misbehaviour (latency, 429/5xx rates, lost responses, receipt delays) is set by its own variables in [cmd/mockprovider/main.go](cmd/mockprovider/main.go). ## Testing ```bash make test ``` - **Go:** `go test -race ./...`. Tests use an embedded Postgres, one fresh database per test, with binaries cached after the first run. Coverage includes the segment compiler and validation, templates and SMS encoding, queue semantics (leases, sweeper, dedup, backoff), SSE replay, LLM retry and repair, and full API flows. These include chaos sending, the rate limit, receipts, resend, scheduling and per-user language. - **Frontend:** `vue-tsc` type check and Vitest for rule, SMS and stream helpers. - **CI:** [GitHub Actions](.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs vet, gofmt, the Go tests with `-race`, the frontend checks and tests, and the Docker build. ## API | Endpoint | Purpose | | --- | --- | | `POST /api/campaigns` | Create a campaign from a brief | | `GET /api/campaigns`, `GET /api/campaigns/{id}` | List / read campaigns | | `POST /api/campaigns/{id}/audience` | Generate the audience rule with the LLM (messages follow automatically) | | `POST /api/campaigns/{id}/audience/refine` | Change the rule with an instruction | | `PUT /api/campaigns/{id}/audience` | Save a hand-edited rule | | `POST /api/campaigns/{id}/content` | Regenerate messages (streams to `/events`) | | `PUT /api/campaigns/{id}/content` | Save hand-edited messages | | `POST /api/campaigns/{id}/approve` | Queue one delivery per consenting recipient and channel; `{"send_at": …}` schedules it | | `POST /api/campaigns/{id}/unschedule` | Cancel a scheduled campaign before it starts | | `POST /api/campaigns/{id}/resend` | Send again what did not arrive (a new round; invalid contacts skipped) | | `GET /api/campaigns/{id}/events` | Server-sent events: status changes, message text as it is written, delivery progress | | `GET /api/campaigns/{id}/deliveries[/counts]` | Delivery list (filter by `status`) and counts | | `GET /api/segments/fields`, `POST /api/segments/preview` | Rule fields; preview counts for a rule | | `GET /api/deliveries/recent` | Status codes of the latest deliveries (the home page band) | | `POST /webhooks/provider` | Signed delivery receipts from the provider | Errors are JSON: `{"error": {"code", "message", "problems": [...]}}`. ## Project layout ``` cmd/server API, workers and web app in one binary cmd/mockprovider fake SMS/email provider with signed receipts internal/api HTTP handlers, SSE streams, webhooks, middleware internal/campaign campaign lifecycle: audience, content, approve, schedule, resend, progress, translations internal/composer prompts and LLM calls for audience, messages and translation; streaming field extractor; mock LLM internal/segment rule model, field catalog, validation, SQL compiler, preview, plain-language description internal/message templates: variables, rendering, worst-case length, GSM-7/UCS-2 internal/delivery sender (rate limit, retries, idempotency), provider client, receipts internal/queue Postgres job queue and workers internal/events event log, LISTEN/NOTIFY hub, SSE deltas internal/llm provider interface, Anthropic client, retry; llmtest fake internal/store pgx pool, embedded Postgres, migrations internal/… backoff, config, metrics, schema, seed, testdb, webhook signatures web/ Vue 3 + Vite + Tailwind v4 frontend tools/sessionexport scrubber for the AI session exports ``` ## Bonus features - **CI:** GitHub Actions, described above. - **Scheduled sending:** pick a time at approval, and cancel it any time before it starts. - **Each user in their own language:** one AI translation per language in the audience, not per user, checked against the same limits. A failed translation falls back to the original. A/B variants were left out on purpose: without opens or clicks there is nothing to compare. Details are in [DECISIONS.md › Bonus features](DECISIONS.md#bonus-features). ## Known limitations - Built for thousands of users, not millions. [DECISIONS.md › Known limits at high scale](DECISIONS.md#known-limits-at-high-scale) covers what breaks first at a million, with measurements, and the fix for each. - The rate limiter is per process. Several replicas would need a shared limiter. - Mock data only: users are generated, and the provider is a simulation. - No authentication. It is a single-tenant demo. ## AI sessions The Claude Code sessions used to build this are in [ai-sessions/](ai-sessions/), with keys and personal data scrubbed.

# Build plan

The core flow comes first: brief → audience → messages → approval → sending → live dashboard. Every phase ends
with passing tests and something that runs. Bonus features start only after the core flow works end to end in
`docker compose up`.

## Architecture

## Phases

| # | Phase | Done when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Infra port: database ✓, config, HTTP helpers, backoff, schema validator, event hub + SSE, queue | Tests pass |
| 1 | Data + seed: migrations, deterministic seeder (Turkish cities and names, realistic consent mix) | `make run` seeds 5,000 users once |
| 2 | Segment engine + preview endpoint | Rule → counts, fully tested |
| 3 | LLM layer + audience generation (repair loop, mock composer) | Brief → validated rule, with or without a key |
| 4 | Messages: templates, streaming generation, edits | Streamed, validated copy |
| 5 | Sending: approve, mock provider, workers, retries, metrics | E2E test: exactly-once delivery under errors |
| 6 | Live stream for the dashboard | Counts update live over SSE |
| 7 | Frontend | Whole flow in the browser |
| 8 | Packaging + docs: Dockerfile with web build, compose, README with diagram, DECISIONS, session export | `docker compose up` on a clean machine |
| 9 | Bonus, in order: scheduled sending (`run_at` already exists), CI, A/B variants, per-user language | — |

If time gets short, cut in this order: A/B variants, frontend tests, chip editing (keep "refine" only).

## Decisions taken

1. **One language per campaign.** Copy is written in the brief's language by default, and the marketer can pick
   another. Sending each user their own language stays a bonus item.
2. **Audience editing:** edit values or remove conditions on the rule chips, plus a "refine" box that sends an
   instruction back to Claude with the current rule. Every edit goes through the same validation.
3. **Delivery status comes from provider webhooks.** Statuses: `queued`, `sending`, `retrying`, `sent`
   (accepted), then `delivered` or `undelivered` from the webhook; `failed` when our sending gives up.
4. **All external data is mock data, kept minimal.** No event-history table: the seed sets the last cart and
   purchase dates on each user. Users' language is stored for a later "translate per user" step.
5. **Model:** `claude-haiku-5-5` by default for cheap manual testing, changeable with `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`.

## Reused from my earlier projects

The infrastructure was ported from my own projects and adapted:

- **Database layer:** `pgx` pool, embedded Postgres fallback, migrations, one database per test.
- **HTTP helpers and config:** strict JSON decoding, JSON errors, access logs, panic recovery, and a `.env`
  allowlist.
- **JSON Schema validator.**
- **Event hub and SSE stream:** generalised from "agent runs" to any topic.
- **Lease-based queue pattern.**
- **LLM interface and retry:** planned next.

What changed in the port, and why:

- **Queue leases have no heartbeat.** The original ran long agent jobs that needed one. Here each job is one
  provider call, so the handler's context ends before the lease does (lease 30 s). A crashed worker's job is
  requeued by the sweeper. The provider idempotency key covers the one gap left: the provider accepted a message,
  but the worker died before saving that.
- **One generic `jobs` table instead of a per-domain queue.** Sending, content generation and scheduled sends all
  use it; `run_at` doubles as the scheduling field.
- **Embedded Postgres binaries are unpacked once per machine** for tests, in the user cache folder, under a file
  lock. Unpacking took about 60 s per test package under `-race`; now the whole suite runs in seconds.

----

- **Official Anthropic Go SDK** behind a small `Provider` interface (ported from my earlier project). Every call
  streams.
- **JSON comes from structured outputs** (`output_config.format`), not a forced tool call. Newer models reject
  forced `tool_choice`, and structured outputs keep the answer's shape fixed.
- **The backend validates what the schema can't express:** known fields and values, number ranges, and later
  message lengths.
- **One retry policy.** The SDK's own retries are off, and ours retries 429/5xx/529 with backoff and jitter,
  honoring `Retry-After`. Errors after text has streamed are never retried, so an answer is never shown twice.
- **One repair round.** If the answer fails validation, Claude gets one fresh request with the rejected answer and
  every problem listed. A second failure is shown to the marketer, who can reword the brief or edit the rule by
  hand. The rejected answer is quoted in a new user message, not replayed as an assistant turn, which keeps
  requests valid under newer models' history checks.
----
## Messages

- **One language per campaign**, `tr` or `en`. By default the model uses the brief's language. If the marketer
  picks one, the schema's `language` enum is narrowed to it, so the model cannot answer in another.
- **Limits are checked after personalization against this audience,** not the template alone. The backend reads
  the longest first name, last name and city among the matched users and renders the worst case. An SMS that fits
  for "Ankara" can be too long for "Eskişehir". Changing the audience re-checks existing messages: they become
  `invalid` (with the reason) or stay `ready`, without being rewritten.
- **SMS encoding is reported, not enforced.** The requirement is ≤ 160 characters. Turkish letters (ş, ğ, ı, İ)
  switch an SMS to UCS-2, where one part holds 70 characters, so a 149-character Turkish SMS goes out as 3 parts.
----
